[0056] Examples of the unsaturated monomer having a carboxyl group, which is copolymerized with the monoethylenically unsaturated monomer to form a carboxyl group-containing (meth)acrylic polymer, include acrylic acid, methacrylic acid, maleic acid, itaconic acid, ω-carboxypolycaprolactone monoacrylate, monohydroxyethyl phthalate(meth)acrylate, β-carboxyethyl acrylate, 2-(meth)acryloyloxyethylsuccinic acid, and 2-(meth)acryloyloxyethylhexahydrophthalic acid.

[0057] The carboxyl group-containing (meth)acrylic polymer is preferably obtained by copolymerizing 80 to 95.5 parts by weight of the monoethylenically unsaturated monomer as a main component with 0.5 to 20 parts by weight of the unsaturated monomer having a carboxyl group.

[0058] Examples of the unsaturated monomer having an amino group, which is copolymerized with the monoethylenically unsaturated monomer to form an amino group-containing (meth)acrylic polymer, include dialkylaminoalkyl (meth)acrylates such as N,N-dimethylaminoethyl acrylate (DMAEA) and N,N-dimethylaminoethyl methacrylate (DMAEMA); dialkylaminoalkyl (meth)acrylamides such as N,N-dimethylaminopropylacrylamide (DMAPAA) and N,N-dimethylaminopropylmethacrylamide; and monomers having a tertiary amino group represented by vinyl monomer having a nitrogen-containing heterocycle such as vinylimidazole.

[0059] The amino group-containing (meth)acrylic polymer is preferably obtained by copolymerizing 80 to 95.5 parts by weight of the monoethylenically unsaturated monomer as a main component with 0.5 to 20 parts by weight of the unsaturated monomer having an amino group.

[0060] After the carboxyl group-containing (meth)acrylic polymer and the amino group-containing (meth)acrylic polymer were separately polymerized as described above, a (meth)acrylic film of the present invention can be formed by a conventional film forming method. Specifically, the film can be formed by mixing solutions of these polymers, applying the mixed solution on the release surface of a liner, and solidifying the solution with drying. As a coating device, there can be used conventional coaters such as bar coater, knife coater, roll coater, and die coater. The solidifying operation is the same as the operation of cooling the molten resin component. Also this film can be formed by a melt extrusion molding method.

[0061] A film having desired tensile strength and elongation characteristics can be obtained by changing a mixing ratio of the carboxyl group-containing (meth)acrylic polymer to the amino group-containing (meth)acrylic polymer in the formation of the film. Specifically, a mixing ratio of a polymer having high Tg to a polymer having low Tg among the carboxyl group-containing (meth)acrylic polymer and the amino group-containing (meth)acrylic polymer is preferably within a range from 10:90 to 90:10, more preferably from 20:80 to 90:10, and most preferably from 30:70 to 90:10. It is preferable to increase the amount of the polymer having high Tg.

[0062] It is preferable to crosslink the carboxyl group-containing (meth)acrylic polymer and the amino group-containing (meth)acrylic polymer in the formation of the film. By crosslinking them, networks are formed, and then it contributes to improve low temperature flexibility. As a crosslinker, a crosslinking agent containing functional groups that can react with carboxylic groups is used. Specifically, bisamide (for example, RD1054 made by 3M), azirizine (for example, Chemitite PZ33 made by Nihon Shokubai, NeoCryl CX-100 made by Avecia), carbodiimide (for example, Carbodilite V-03, V-05, V-07 made by Nisshinbo), epoxy (for example, E-AX, E-5XM, E5C made by Soken Chemical & Engineering) are used. An amount of the crosslinking agent is from 0.1 to 5 parts by weight for 100 parts by weight of the carboxyl group-containing (meth)acrylic polymer.

[0063] In the (meth)acrylic film of the present invention, the tensile strength is preferably 3 MPa or more, more preferably 15 MPa or more, and most preferably 30 MPa or more. When the tensile strength is less than 3 MPa, there arises a problem that the resulting film is likely to be broken when applied on the adherend. In the (meth)acrylic film of the present invention, the elongation is preferably 25% or more, more preferably 50% or more, and most preferably 75% or more. When the elongation is less than 25%, there arises a problem that the resulting film is likely to be broken when applied on the adherend.

[0064] The tensile strength and elongation are measured under the following conditions in accordance with the method defined in JIS K6251.
Shape of sample to be measured: “dumbbell shaped No. 3 test piece” defined in JIS K6251
Testing speed: 300 min/min
Measuring temperature: 5° C. and 25° C.

[0068] The measured results were summarized as follows.
Tensile Strength T (unit: MPa)

[0069] After measuring a maximum tensile force F (unit: N) up to breakage of a test piece and a cross section A (unit: mm2) of the test piece, the tensile strength was determined by the following equation.
T=F/A
Elongation E (unit: %)

[0070] After measuring a distance between marked lines L1 (unit: mm) upon breakage and a distance between marked lines L0 (25 mm) of a test piece, the elongation was determined by the following equation.
E=(L1−L0)/L0×100

[0071] The thickness of the (meth)acrylic film of the present invention is not specifically limited and can be controlled to the same thickness as that of a conventional decorative sheet. Specifically, the thickness is generally within a range from 1 to 1000 μm, preferably from 5 to 500 μm, and more preferably from 20 to 150 μm, although it varies depending on the purposes. When the thickness is too large, the mechanical strength decreases and the resulting film is likely to be broken when the film is peeled after bonding to the adherend. On the other hand, when the thickness is too large, the flexibility of the film is likely to be deteriorated.

[0072] The (meth)acrylic film of the present invention is excellent in weatherability as compared with a commercially available vinyl chloride film, and also the surface gloss retention and color difference after an accelerated aging test are the same as or better than those of the vinyl chloride film.

[0073] The surface gloss retention and color difference are measured according to the following procedure.

[0074] First, an acrylic adhesive of an isooctyl acrylate-methyl acrylate-acrylic acid copolymer in a ratio of 70:22.5:7.5 (weight ratio) (solvent: ethyl acetate, weight-average molecular weight: 360,000, Tg: −7° C.) was prepared. An adhesive composition was prepared by mixing 100 parts by weight of the acrylic adhesive with 1.7 parts by weight (solid content ratio) of a bisamide crosslinking agent, applied on a release paper comprising a paper base and a polyethylene laminate formed on both surfaces of the paper base using a knife coater so that the resulting film has a thickness of 30 μm after drying, and then dried and crosslinked with heating at 90° C. for 5 minutes. Then, a film to be measured such as (meth)acrylic film was laminated thereon to obtain a test piece. After test piece was applied on a 1 mm thick aluminum plate (A5082P) and allowed to stand for 200 hours in a weatherometer (KU-R5C1-A) manufactured by DAIPLA WINTES CO., LTD., the surface gloss retention and color difference were measured. The test piece was irradiated with light at a dose of 60 mW/cm2 while repeating a cycle of lighting at a temperature of 60° C. and a humidity of 50% for 4 hours and lights-out at a temperature of 40° C. and a humidity of 98% for 4 hours.

[0075] Using a portable gloss meter (GMX-202, manufactured by MURAKAMI COLOR RESEARCH LABORATORY), 60° surface gloss was measured. The surface gloss retention was calculated by the following equation.
[Surface gloss retention (%)]={[Surface gloss after irradiation]−[Surface gloss before irradiation]}×100

[0076] Using a color meter (Σ90, manufactured by NIPPON DENSHOKU Co., Ltd.), L*, a* and b* were measured. The color difference was calculated by the following equation:
[Color difference]=[(L 2 *−L 1*)2+(a 2 *−a 1*)2+(b 2 *−B 1*)2]1/2
where L1*, a1* and b1* are measured values before irradiation, and L2*, a2* and b2* are measured values after irradiation.

[0077] To the film, hiding pigments can be added when hiding properties are required. If necessary, one or more conventionally known additives such as antioxidants, ultraviolet absorbers, photostabilizers, plasticizers, lubricants, antistatic agents, flame retardants, and fillers may be added according to the purposes of the film.
Marking Film

[0078] Preferred example of the marking film of the present invention will be described with reference to FIG. 1. FIG. 1 is a cross-sectional view showing schematically the marking film of the present invention. A (meth)acrylic film (1) in a marking film (100) has a surface (11) and a back surface (12) and receives a colorant received on the surface (11), namely, a toner (2). In order to prevent the toner from falling off, a protective film (3) can be provided on the surface of the film. In this case, the toner (2) forms a visible image from the outermost surface (31) of the protective film (3) through the protective film (3). Also adhesion between the toner (2) and the (meth)acrylic film (1) can be enhanced by providing a receptor layer (5) on the surface (11) of the (meth)acrylic film (1).

[0079] On the back surface (12) of the meth)acrylic film (1), an adhesive layer (4) is fixedly provided. The adhesive layer usually forms a flat adhesive surface, but it may have an uneven adhesive surface. On the uneven adhesive surface (41) of the adhesive layer (4), a protruding portion (not shown) and a recessed portion (not shown) surrounding the protruding portion are formed. The unevenness of the adhesive surface is designed to include grooves capable of forming a communicating passage to the edge of the adhesive sheet when the adhesive sheet is bonded to an adherend.

[0080] As the (meth)acrylic film (1), the above-mentioned the (meth)acrylic film is used. The colorant is usually a toner or ink. The toner comprises a binder resin and a pigment dispersed in the binder resin. The binder resin is composed of a mixture of one or more kinds selected from the group consisting of vinyl chloride-vinyl acetate copolymer, an acrylic resin and polyester resin.

[0081] The entire protective film (3) has light transmission properties. A light transmission is usually 60% or more, preferably 70% or more, and particularly preferably 80% or more. The term “light transmission” as used herein means an entire light transmission as measured by a spectrophotometer or, a color meter which also serves as a photometer, using light having a wavelength of 550 nm.

[0082] The protective film (3) is preferably made of a resin film containing high transparency. The resin of the resin film includes, for example, fluororesin, phthalate polyester (e.g. PET and PEN), acrylic resin, and petroleum-resistant resin. The fluororesin is a polymer obtained by polymerizing the fluorine monomer. The fluorine monomer includes, for example, fluorine ethylene monomers such as vinylidene fluoride, propylene hexafluorine, ethylene tetrafluoride, and ethylene chloride trifluoride. It is possible to mix one or more kinds of copolymerizable monomers selected from methacrylates such as methyl methacrylate, ethyl methacrylate, propyl methacrylate, and butyl methacrylate; and acrylates such as methyl acrylate, ethyl acrylate, propyl acrylate, and butyl acrylate, in addition to the fluorine monomer. Also a protective film may be made of a resin composition obtained by blending the fluorine resin with the acrylic resin. The thickness of the protective film is usually within a range from 5 to 120 μm, and preferably from 10 to 100 μm.

[0083] An adhesive layer for protective film (30) is usually used to bond the protective film (3) to the (meth)acrylic film (1). The adhesive of the adhesive layer for protective film (30) is not specifically limited, but is usually a pressure-sensitive adhesive containing an adhesive polymer by the following reason. That is, the pressure-sensitive adhesive satisfactorily conforms to the unevenness formed by the toner (2) in the surface (11) of the (meth)acrylic film, thereby making it possible to make the protective film (3) and the (meth)acrylic film (1) come closely into contact with each other without leaving bubbles therebetween. It is preferable so as not to leave bubbles because bubbles impair the visibility. The thickness of the adhesive layer for protective film (30) is usually within a range from 20 to 100 μm, and preferably from 25 to 80 μm.

[0084] The resin constituting the receptor layer (5) is not specifically limited and there can be used acrylic polymer, polyolefin, polyvinyl acetal and phenoxy resin. The glass transition temperature of the resin constituting the receptor layer is usually within a range from 0 to 100° C. When the glass transition temperature of the receptor layer is too high, the toner transferrability is lowered and a clear image may not be obtained. Furthermore, when the glass transition temperature of the receptor layer is too high, the flexibility of the entire marking film may be lowered. The glass transition temperature of the receptor layer is preferably adjusted to 0° C. or higher in order to effectively lower tack at normal temperature of the surface of receiving the colorant. Consequently, it is made possible to effectively prevent sticking of marking film precursors and receptor sheets before coating with the protective film. Therefore, after stored in the form of a roll, the roll can be used easily while unwinding. The thickness of the receptor layer is usually within a range from 20 to 50 μm, and preferably from 5 to 40 μm.

[0085] The adhesive of the adhesive layer (4) is not specifically limited and is usually a pressure-sensitive adhesive containing an adhesive polymer. As the pressure-sensitive adhesive layer, for example, a single-layered pressure-sensitive adhesive film containing an adhesive polymer and a double-coated adhesive sheet comprising two pressure-sensitive layers are preferably used.

[0086] The adhesive layer (4) can be made of a coating film of an adhesive containing an adhesive polymer. Preferable adhesive comprises an adhesive polymer and a crosslinking agent containing the adhesive polymer. The term “adhesive polymer” used herein refers to a polymer which exhibits adhesion at normal temperature (about 25° C.). As the adhesive polymer, for example, acrylic polymer, polyurethane, polyolefin and polyester can be used.

[0087] An example of the synthesis of the adhesive polymer will be explained by way of an acrylic polymer. First, a polar (meth)acrylic monomer such as acrylic unsaturated acid (for example, acrylic acid, methacrylic acid, itaconic acid, or maleic acid) or acrylonitrile is prepared as a first monomer. The first monomer is mixed with an acrylic monomer as a second monomer to prepare a monomer mixture. As the second monomer, there can be used alkyl acrylates, for example, isooctyl acrylate, butyl acrylate, 2-methylbutyl acrylate, 2-ethylhexyl acrylate, and isononyl acrylate. Using a solution polymerization, emulsion polymerization or bulk polymerization method, an adhesive polymer having a predetermined molecular weight is synthesized from the mixture thus prepared.

[0088] When using a crosslinking agent in case of crosslinking the adhesive polymer, the amount of the crosslinking agent varies depending on the kind of the crosslinking agent, but is usually within a range from 0.02 to 2 parts by weight, and preferably from 0.03 to 1 parts by weight, based on 100 parts by weight of the adhesive polymer. As the crosslinking agent, for example, there can be used isocyanate compound, melamine compound, poly(meth)acrylate compound, epoxy compound, and amide compound, bisamide compound [bisaziridine derivative of dibasic acid such as isophthaloylbis(2-methylaziridine)].

[0089] The glass transition temperature (Tg) of the adhesive layer is preferably within a range from −50 to 0° C., and more preferably from −45 to −5° C. When Tg of the adhesive layer is too high, adhesion between the adherend and the marking film is likely to be lowered. On the other hand, when Tg of the adhesive layer is too low, when the marking film is stored in the form of a roll, the adhesive oozes from the side portion of the roll and sticking of mutually contacted marking films may not be prevented. Tg is a value determined from Tan ∂measured by using a dynamic viscoelasticity measuring device (Rheometrics Scientific Inc. RDA-II). The measurement was carried out under the conditions of a shear rate of 1 radian/sec (torsion mode), a heating range from −60 to 100° C. and a heating rate of 5° C./sec. The thickness of the specimen is usually from 1 to 2 mm.

[0090] The thickness of the protective film is usually within a range from 5 to 200 μm, preferably from 20 to 100 μm, and more preferably from 25 to 80 μm. As far as the effect of the present invention is not impaired, there can be added additives such as tackifiers, elastic microspheres, adhesive polymer microspheres, crystalline polymers, inorganic powders, and ultraviolet absorbers.

[0091] The adhesive layer (4) usually has a flat adhesive surface, but may have an uneven adhesive surface as described above. An example of a method of forming the uneven adhesive surface will be described.

[0092] First, a liner having a release surface of a predetermined uneven structure is prepared. A coating composition containing an adhesive polymer (adhesive coating composition for forming an adhesive layer of an adhesive sheet) is applied on the release surface of the liner, and then dried to form an adhesive layer. Consequently, a negative structure of the uneven surface of the liner is imparted to the surface of the adhesive layer in contact with the liner. This adhesive surface subsequently serves as the adhesive surface of the adhesive sheet to form an uneven adhesive surface having a predetermined structure (positive structure) on the adhesive surface. The unevenness of the adhesive surface is designed to include grooves capable of forming a communicating passage to the edge of the adhesive sheet when the adhesive sheet is bonded to an adherend, as described above.

[0093] As far as it is possible to prevent bubbles from being trapped during application of the marking film, grooves in the surface of the adhesive layer having a regular or irregular shape may be disposed on the adhesive layer in a regular or irregular pattern to provide grooves having a regular pattern When a plurality of grooves is formed wherein the grooves are generally parallel with each other, the distance between the grooves is preferably from 10 to 2,000 μm. The depth of the grooves (the distance between the adhesive surface and the bottom of the groove measured in the direction of the thickness of the receptor film) is usually from 10 to 100 μm. Also the shape of the groove is not specifically limited so long as the effect of the present invention is not impaired. For example, the groove may have a generally rectangular, trapezoidal, semicircular or semielliptical cross section in a direction perpendicular to the adhesive surface. Alternatively, the groove may have a cross section that is irregular.

[0094] A marking film (100) can be produced in the following manner. First, the above-mentioned (meth)acrylic film (1) is prepared. In case the marking film (100) includes a receptor layer (5), the receptor layer is formed on the liner and the (meth)acrylic film is then formed on the receptor layer with the liner. In this case, as far as the effect of the present invention is not impaired, the other layer, for example, a primer layer or an adhesive layer may be provided between the (meth)acrylic film (1) and the receptor layer (5).

[0095] Then, an adhesive layer (4) is made to come closely into contact with the back surface of the (meth)acrylic film (1). A coating solution containing an adhesive is applied on the release surface of the liner and dried to form an adhesive layer with the liner, and then the adhesive layer wit the liner is laminated on the back surface of the (meth)acrylic film (1), thereby making the adhesive layer come closely into contact with the back surface of the (meth)acrylic film.

[0096] Then, an image is formed on the surface of the (meth)acrylic film (1) by the toner (2) and a protective film (3) is optionally provided thereon, thereby making it possible to complete the marking film (100) of the present invention. In case an image is formed by transferring the toner (2) onto the surface of the (meth)acrylic film (1), the image is formed by transferring the toner using a conventional printing method. In case of using an electrostatic printing method, an image is temporarily formed on a temporary carrier referred to as a transfer media and the image is then transferred onto the surface of the (meth)acrylic film (1) by heating under pressure.

[0097] The thickness of the marking film is usually within a range from 30 to 1500 μm preferably from 50 to 950 μm. When the thickness is too small, the mechanical strength decreases and the marking film is likely to be broken when peeled again after bonding to the adherend. On the other hand, when the thickness is too large, the flexibility of the marking film is likely to be lowered.
Receptor Sheet

[0098] The receptor sheet of the present invention is a film with an adhesive layer, which comprises the (meth)acrylic film to which colorants such as toner are applied, and an adhesive layer which bonds the (meth)acrylic film to an adherend. That is, the receptor sheet does not include the toner (2) and the protective film (3) and is composed of the (meth)acrylic film (1) and the adhesive layer (4). Therefore, the (meth)acrylic film and the adhesive layer can have the same constitution as that of the marking film, and also the same formation methods can be used.

[0099] The total thickness of the receptor sheet is usually within a range from 5 to 1200 μm, and preferably from 25 to 700 μm. When the thickness is too small, the mechanical strength decreases and the receptor sheet is likely to be broken when the marking film is peeled again after bonding to the adherend. On the other hand, when the thickness is too large, the flexibility of the marking film including the receptor sheet is likely to be deteriorated.

eval_task_config.task_instruction: Draft an English response to the U.S. Office Action.

scoring_policy.subjective_metrics: The Judge returns 0, 0.5, or 1 for each scored criterion using its own levels. G3-G5 additionally follow the synchronized zero-score rule below. The Judge does not calculate weights or totals.
scoring_policy.input_mode: Case source materials, task requirements, and the candidate response; no expert annotations or case-specific scoring layer.
scoring_policy.validation_checks: Case identity, input completeness, consultation of legal provisions, and verification of quotations are evaluation checks, not separately weighted criteria.

steps: Distribute the common-layer budget among applicable groups in the ratio foundation:amendment:argument = 25:20:55. If an entire group is not applicable, renormalize the remaining original group budgets.

Within the argument group, distribute its budget among applicable issue types according to argument_types.relative_weight. Inventive step is one complete issue type; its budget does not vary with the number of applicable inventive-step subcriteria.

Within each group other than argument, or within each argument issue type, distribute the budget among applicable criteria in proportion to each criterion's relative_weight. Use unrounded weights throughout the calculation.
weight_allocation.final_score: round(100 * C, 1), only when every applicable criterion is scored
weight_allocation.baseline_warning: The all-applicable percentages are illustrative only. Do not drop inapplicable entries from those percentages and renormalize the resulting flat list.
weight_allocation.calibration_note: These weights are initial design values, not proportions prescribed by the Word standard, and have not yet been calibrated against the new 100-case set.

applicability.amendment_rule: G3-G5 activate together when the candidate actually amends the claims and are scored using the Word levels. If the synchronized zero-score rule applies, all three remain active with score 0. Otherwise, when no amendment is made, all three are not_applicable.
applicability.argument_rule: Determine applicability of each G6 criterion from the complete OA, the actual points of dispute, the jurisdiction, and the necessary reasoning steps. A single inventive-step objection may require several subcriteria. A missing candidate response does not make an existing issue not applicable.
applicability.not_applicable: Use status=not_applicable and score=null only when a conditional criterion does not apply; provide the reason and references to source materials. Only not_applicable releases allocated weight.

amendment_zero_rule.trigger: The Judge determines that the claims should be amended, but the candidate OAR has not chosen an amendment strategy.
amendment_zero_rule.evidence_requirement: Each of G3-G5 must cite the case basis showing why amendment is needed and evidence that the candidate did not choose that strategy. A difference between pre_claim and post_claim alone is insufficient to infer that amendment is required.
amendment_zero_rule.defect_description_requirement: Each criterion's defect description must identify its current metric ID and explain that the zero score is required by this synchronized rule.
amendment_zero_rule.scope: Do not mark these three criteria not_applicable or redistribute the amendment budget. G2, G6, and all other scoring rules continue to apply as specified.

result_contract.scored: A score of 0, 0.5, or 1 and verifiable evidence references are required.
result_contract.unscored: not_applicable, not_evaluable, and failed require score=null. Conditional not_applicable results require a reason and source references.
result_contract.failure_handling: not_evaluable and failed retain their allocated shares and block the final score. Do not redistribute their shares to scored criteria or remove an inventive-step type because one subcriterion cannot be evaluated.
result_contract.consistency_checks: Validate required criteria, consistent applicability of G3-G5, compliance with the synchronized zero-score rule, and evidence fields. Programmatic checks do not replace semantic review.

audit_fields.common_group_allocation: Group budgets, active criteria, and argument.types with issue-type budgets and subcriteria.
audit_fields.common_allocated_weights: Allocated weights including shares reserved for not_evaluable or failed criteria.
audit_fields.common_effective_weights: Weights actually contributing to the score; not_applicable, not_evaluable, and failed have effective weight 0. Failed or unevaluable applicable criteria still block a final total.

scoring_policy.duplicate_defect_rule: Assign each minimal defect to one primary criterion rather than penalizing it repeatedly across criteria. The explicitly required synchronized G3-G5 zero scores are a policy exception; each must identify the current criterion and the reason for the rule-based zero score.

metrics.name: Accuracy of understanding the case facts and Office Action
metrics.evaluation_object: Whether the application, its current claims, the Office Action, and the relevant cited documents are correctly understood, and whether the validity of the grounds for objection is correctly assessed.

levels.1: Correctly understands the application, the claims, the technical features, and their relationships; accurately understands the meaning of the grounds for objection and accurately assesses whether they are valid.
levels.0.5: Correctly assesses the main technical solution, the grounds for objection, and the points open to argument, but has localized misunderstandings of noncritical facts, feature relationships, or document content; these do not change the main direction of the response and can be corrected locally.
levels.0: Misunderstands the technical solution of the application, feature relationships, or the Office Action; makes errors such as confusing the original claims, the current claims, and the proposed amended claims.

metrics.activation_condition: Required for every case.

metrics.name: Reasonableness of the overall response strategy
metrics.evaluation_object: Whether the choice between relying solely on argument and proactively amending the claims is reasonable; if proactive amendment is chosen, whether the choice of claims to amend is reasonable and whether any improper admissions are made.

levels.1: The choice of argument alone, amendment, or a combination of the two is supported by the case; the claims selected for treatment are appropriate, and the overall strategy addresses the core issues in the Office Action; no unsupported, materially adverse admissions are made.
levels.0.5: The main response approach is reasonable, but there are localized inappropriate choices in the treatment of noncore claims that do not affect the main position.
levels.0: The main response approach cannot address the core issues, for example, persisting with argument alone when the arguments lack a valid basis, or failing to include core claims requiring amendment in the strategy; makes adverse admissions that lack a basis in the Office Action and materially weaken the position on the main scope of protection.

metrics.activation_condition: Required for every case.

metrics.name: Effectiveness of claim amendments in addressing the issues identified in the Office Action [if amended]
metrics.evaluation_object: Whether the claim amendments themselves resolve the issues targeted by the Office Action, assessed separately from the quality of the response statement.

levels.1: The specific amendments correspond to the issues identified in the Office Action, and the amended claims, together with the response statement, are sufficient to overcome those defects.
levels.0.5: The amendments resolve the core defects identified in the Office Action, but the treatment of noncore defects is incomplete and requires localized correction.
levels.0: The core defects identified in the Office Action remain after amendment; or the amendments have no substantive connection to the defects identified in the Office Action.

metrics.name: Proportionality of claim amendments and preservation of the scope of protection [if amended]
metrics.evaluation_object: Whether there is avoidable loss of protection while reasonably addressing the Office Action, assessed against the original protection objectives of the case.

levels.1: Added limitations, claim deletions, and other scope adjustments are reasonably necessary or reflect supported strategic tradeoffs; there is no unnecessary narrowing that can be clearly demonstrated from the case materials.
levels.0.5: There are individual unnecessary additional limitations or losses of noncore claims, but the main protection objectives of the original application are not materially affected; a less restrictive and equally reasonable localized adjustment can be specifically identified.
levels.0: Despite the existence of a supported, reasonable approach involving less narrowing, introduces significantly unnecessary limitations, deletes important claims, or abandons key protected subject matter, materially harming the main protection objectives.

metrics.evaluation_object: Whether amendments have a basis in the original disclosure and comply with amendment rules; whether clarity, support, antecedent basis, and claim dependencies meet the applicable requirements.

levels.0: The amendments exceed the permissible scope, introduce content or combinations lacking a basis in the original disclosure, or create generalizations unsupported by the description; substantive errors in key wording, feature relationships, or claim dependencies make the scope of protection indeterminate or the technical solution untenable.

See Column 4, lines 63-68. ***Double Patenting*** The nonstatutory double patenting rejection is based on a judicially created doctrine grounded in public policy (a policy reflected in the statute) so as to prevent the unjustified or improper timewise extension of the "right to exclude" granted by a patent and to prevent possible harassment by multiple assignees. A nonstatutory obviousness-type double patenting rejection is appropriate where the conflicting claims are not identical, but at least one examined application claim is not patentably distinct from the reference claim(s) because the examined application claim is either anticipated by, or would have been obvious over, the reference claim(s). See, e.g., *In re Berg*, 140 F.3d 1428, 46 USPQ2d 1226 (Fed. Cir. 1998); *In re Goodman*, 11 F.3d 1046, 29 USPQ2d 2010 (Fed. Cir. 1993); *In re Longi*, 759 F.2d 887, 225 USPQ 645 (Fed. Cir. 1985); *In re Van Ornum*, 686 F.2d 937, 214 USPQ 761 (CCPA 1982); *In re Vogel*, 422 F.2d 438, 164 USPQ 619 (CCPA 1970); and *In re Thorington*, 418 F.2d 528, 163 USPQ 644 (CCPA 1969). A timely filed terminal disclaimer in compliance with 37 CFR 1.321(c) or 1.321(d) may be used to overcome an actual or provisional rejection based on a nonstatutory --- Application/Control Number: 13/221,391 Art Unit: 3633 Page 7 double patenting ground provided the conflicting application or patent either is shown to be commonly owned with this application, or claims an invention made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of a joint research agreement. Effective January 1, 1994, a registered attorney or agent of record may sign a terminal disclaimer. A terminal disclaimer signed by the assignee must fully comply with 37 CFR 3.73(b). field_values.desc:
# BACKED PANEL AND SYSTEM FOR CONNECTING BACKED PANELS

[0001] This application is a continuation of U.S. Application No. 11/233,929, filed
September 23, 2005, which is hereby incorporated by reference in its entirety.
BACKGROUND AND SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION
[0002] The present invention relates generally to panels and, more particularly, to
a backed panel and a backed panel assembly. Examples of panels that may benefit
from the present invention include siding panels, wall panels, and other similar, suitable,
or conventional types of panels or components. U.S. Patent No. 6,321,500 is hereby
incorporated by reference as just one example of a panel that may benefit from the
present invention. Although the present invention may be described herein primarily
with regard to siding panels and wall panels, it is not intended to limit the present
invention to any particular type of panel or component, unless expressly claimed
otherwise.
[0003] In order to enhance the thermal insulation of building structures, one or
more layers or panels of insulating material may be provided between a facing panel
and a building structure. Known insulated siding systems exist in many different forms.
A common problem with known insulated siding systems is the joint between the sides
of adjacent siding units. Simply abutting siding units that are situated side-by-side may
leave an unsightly gap that may be infiltrated by wind, rain, and insects. On the other
hand, overlapping the siding panels of adjacent backed siding units may result in an
1

uneven or raised seam as a result of the presence of the backing panels. A raised or
uneven seam may also detract from the appearance of the siding and create a passage
for the undesired transfer of air, moisture, and insects. In addition, a raised or uneven
seam may increase the risk of oil canning of the siding panels as well as delamination of
the siding units. Furthermore, overlapping the siding panels may cause breakage or
other damage to the underlying backing panel, which compromises the functionality of
the backing panel. Thus, to achieve the desired level of integration between adjoined
backed paneling units, an improved system and method of forming a lapped joint
between backed panels without interference of the backing panels is needed.
[0004] The present invention provides a backed panel and a system for
connecting backed panels. An exemplary embodiment of the backed panel comprises a
facing panel and a backing panel, wherein the backing panel has a groove, recessed
portion, or any other suitable type of relief channel. An exemplary embodiment of the
relief channel may be adapted to receive a side edge portion of a facing panel of an
adjacent backed panel. By providing a space to receive a side edge portion of an
adjacent facing panel, an exemplary embodiment of the present invention may enable
an improved lap joint to be established between adjacent backed panels.
[0005] In addition to the novel features and advantages mentioned above, other
features and advantages of the present invention will be readily apparent from the
following descriptions of the drawings and exemplary embodiments.
BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE DRAWINGS
[0006] Figure 1 is a partial perspective view of an exemplary embodiment of a
backed panel of the present invention.
2

[0007] Figure 2 is a partial perspective view of a panel assembly including the
backed panel of Figure 1.
[0008] Figure 3 is a partial perspective view of the backing panel of Figure 1.
[0009] Figure 4 is a rear elevation view of an exemplary embodiment of a backed
panel of the present invention (approximate dimensions are given for the purpose of
example only).
[0010] Figure 5 is a partial rear elevation view of the backed panel of Figure 4
(approximate dimensions are given for the purpose of example only).
[0011] Figure 6A is a side elevation view of the backing panel of Figure 4
(approximate dimensions are given for the purpose of example only).
[0012] Figure 6B is another side elevation view of the backing panel of Figure 4
(approximate dimensions are given for the purpose of example only).
[0013] Figure 7 is a partial front elevation view of the backing panel of Figure 4
(approximate dimensions are given for the purpose of example only).
[0014] Figure 8 is a partial bottom plan view of the backing panel of Figure 4
(approximate dimensions are given for the purpose of example only).
[0015] Figure 9 is another side elevation view of the backing panel of Figure 4
(approximate dimensions are given for the purpose of example only).
DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF EXEMPLARY EMBODIMENT(S)
[0016] The present invention is directed to a backed paneling unit. In Figure 1,
an exemplary embodiment of a backed paneling unit 10 (e.g., a siding unit) includes
backing panel or portion 20 and facing panel or portion 30 (e.g., a siding panel), which
may optionally have an attachment flange 32. Side edge portion 22 of backing panel 20
3

includes a relief channel 24. Relief channel 24 may be a groove, channel, or any other
suitable type of recessed portion. In particular, relief channel 24 is adapted to provide a
gap or space between backing panel 20 and siding panel 30 for receiving a side edge
portion of a siding panel of an adjacent siding unit. As a result, an exemplary
embodiment of the present invention may enable the formation of an improved lap
between adjacent backed paneling units.
[0017] Figure 2 shows an example of an assembly including siding unit 10 of
Figure 1. In this example, a lap joint is formed between siding unit 10 and siding unit
40. In particular, a side edge portion 44 of siding panel 42 of siding unit 40 is inserted
into the gap between backing panel 20 and siding panel 30 that is provided by relief
channel 24. Side edge portion 44 of siding panel 42 is shown in phantom because it is
overlapped by siding panel 30.
[0018] Due to relief channel 24, an exemplary embodiment of the present
invention may enable the formation of an improved seam between backed panels that
are located side-by-side. For instance, an exemplary embodiment of the present
invention may enable the seam to be significantly smoother as compared to a backed
panel system that does not include a relief channel in a backing panel. In other words,
displacement of siding panel 30 by side edge portion 44 may be minimized because of
relief channel 24. Thus, in addition to providing a seam that may be resistant to water,
air, and insect infiltration, an exemplary embodiment of the present invention may
enable the formation of a seam that may improve the appearance of a siding assembly
and may also mitigate delamination and oil canning of a siding unit. Furthermore, relief
channel 24 may also limit damage to backing panel 20. In particular, relief channel 24
4

creates a gap that facilitates the insertion of side edge portion 44 under siding panel 30
without damaging backing panel 20.
[0019] Backing panel 20 may be comprised of any suitable material. For
example, backing panel 20 may be comprised of a foamed plastic (e.g., expanded or
extruded polystyrene foam, polyurethane foam, or any other desired plastic foam
material) or any other similar or suitable reinforcing or insulating material. In fact, it
should be recognized that backing panel 20 may be comprised of any material having
desired physical characteristics including, but not limited to, foam, fiberglass, cardboard,
and other similar or suitable materials. Any suitable means may be used to obtain the
shape of backing panel 20. In an exemplary embodiment, the shape of backing panel
20 may be obtained by molding (e.g., compression molding, injection molding, vacuum
molding, or other similar or suitable types of molding), by extrusion through a
predetermined die configuration, by cutting or machining such as with a power saw or
other cutting devices, and/or by any other suitable method.
[0020] Siding panel 30 may be comprised of any suitable material. An exemplary
embodiment of siding panel 30 may be formed from a polymer such as a vinyl material.
Other materials such as polypropylene,polyethylene, other plastics and polymers,
polymer composites (such as polymer reinforced with fibers or other particles of glass,
graphite, wood, flax, other cellulosic materials, or other inorganic or organic materials),
metals (such as aluminum or polymer coated metal), or other similar or suitable
materials may also be used. The panel may be molded, extruded, roll-formed from a
flat sheet, or formed by any other suitable manufacturing technique.
5

[0021] Backing panel 20, which may, for example, be used for panel stiffness,
reinforcement, thermal insulation, noise mitigation, or reduction of oil canning, may be
attached to the backside of siding panel 30. Attachment of the backing panel 20 to the
siding panel 30 may be achieved using any desired attachment material. Examples of
attachment materials include adhesives, glues, epoxies, polymers, tapes (pressure
sensitive adhesive tapes), VELCRO, other hook and loop fastening materials, and other
similar or suitable attachment materials. For example, an adhesive may be used to
bond a portion of backing panel 20 to a portion of the inside of siding panel 30. In one
exemplary embodiment, the attachment material may be flexible such that it may help to
compensate for the expansion and contraction forces between backing panel 20 and
siding panel 30, which may expand and contract at different rates.
[0022] Optionally, such as shown in Figure 3, backing panel 20 may include
grooves 26 to enhance attachment of backing panel 20 to siding panel 30. Grooves 26
may provide space between backing panel 20 and siding panel 30 to accept and retain
a desired quantity of an attachment material to promote attachment. Grooves 26 may
be machined, extruded, molded, or imparted into backing panel 20 by any suitable
method and in any desired direction(s). For example, grooves 26 may be selectively
positioned to provide direction for optimal placement of the attachment material for
attaching backing panel 20 to siding panel 30. In this example, grooves 26 extend in a
generally horizontal direction substantially across the entire length of backing panel 20
to account for forces in the longitudinal direction of siding unit 10 caused by the different
expansion and contraction properties of backing panel 20 and siding panel 30.
Although grooves 26 stop at relief channel 24 in this example, grooves 26 may
6

optionally extend through relief channel 24. Other variations are also possible. For
example, in other exemplary embodiments of the present invention, grooves 26 may:
only extend a limited distance; extend in a vertical, diagonal, or other desired direction;
have a winding or other curvy shape; intersect with at least one other recess; and/or
extend along any other desired direction.
[0023] Referring now to the example shown in Figures 4 and 5, siding unit 50 is
comprised of a backing panel 60 and a siding panel 70. Relief channels 62, which are
shown in phantom, are provided on opposing side edge portions of backing panel 60 in
this exemplary embodiment. However, in other exemplary embodiments of the present
invention, a relief channel may optionally be provided on only one side edge portion. A
relief channel 62 may extend along any desired portion of a side edge portion of
backing panel 60. In this example, a relief channel may extend from the bottom of
backing panel 60 up to a point approximately where backing panel 60 is proximate to an
attachment flange of siding panel 70. Figure 1 shows another example of this type of
configuration. Nevertheless, it should be recognized that a relief channel of other
exemplary embodiments may extend along a different portion of the side edge portion
or along the entire side edge portion of the backing panel.
[0024] A relief channel 62 may have any suitable dimensions that enable it to
receive an adjacent siding panel. In Figures 4 and 5, the dimensions, which are in
inches, are provided merely as an example of one embodiment of the present invention.
Figure 5 is a detail of Figure 4 showing exemplary dimensions of a relief channel 62.
Optionally, such as shown in Figure 5, backing panel 60 may be offset from the side
edge of siding panel 70, which may also facilitate the formation of a lap joint with an
7

adjacent siding unit. In this example, the offset may be about 0.625 inch. Nevertheless,
it should be recognized that the optional offset may be any suitable or desired distance.
Furthermore, as shown in Figure 5, a relief channel 62 in this example may have a
depth of about 1.0 inch. However, it should again be recognized that any suitable depth
may be selected for relief channel 62 to enable it to receive an adjacent siding panel.
[0025] Figures 6A, 6B, 7, 8, and 9 illustrate further exemplary dimensions for
backing panel 60. Again, it should be recognized that such dimensions are provided for
illustrative purposes only and are not intended to limit the invention unless expressly
claimed otherwise. Figure 7 shows that relief channel 62 starts about 1.145 inches from
the top edge of backing panel 60 in this exemplary embodiment. In addition, Figures 7
and 8 more clearly show the approximate 1.0-inch depth of relief channel 62 of this
example, and Figures 8 and 9 show that the approximate width of this exemplary
embodiment of relief channel 62 is about 0.05 inch. As shown in Figures 7 and 8, relief
channel 62 may have a chamfer 64 along any portion of its side edge. In this example,
chamfer 64 extends along the entire side edge of relief channel 62. Chamfer 64 may
facilitate the insertion of an adjacent siding panel into relief channel 62. In addition,
chamfer 64 may also help to limit damage to the side edge of relief channel 62, which
could be caused the insertion of an adjacent siding panel into relief channel 62. A
chamfer may have any suitable dimensions. In this example, chamfer 64 has a depth of
about 0.125 inch, and it extends at about a 22-degree angle from the primary surface of
relief channel 62. Other dimensions for chamfer 64 are possible and considered within
the scope of the present invention. Backing panel 60 may also include optional grooves
66 such as shown in Figure 7, which may provide space between backing panel 60 and
8

siding panel 70 to accept and retain a desired quantity of an attachment material to
promote attachment of backing panel 60 to siding panel 70. As shown in Figures 8 and
9, the profile of this exemplary embodiment backing panel 60 may have a slight radius
curvature of about 100.0235 inches, whereas the radius curvature of relief channel 62
may be about 100.0735 in this example. The radius curvature of a backing panel and
relief channel of the present invention may be selected to obtain the desired aesthetic,
physical, and performance characteristics of the backing panel and overall siding unit.
[0026] Any embodiment of the present invention may include any of the optional
or preferred features of the other embodiments of the present invention. The exemplary
embodiments herein disclosed are not intended to be exhaustive or to unnecessarily
limit the scope of the invention. The exemplary embodiments were chosen and
described in order to explain the principles of the present invention so that others skilled
in the art may practice the invention. Having shown and described exemplary
embodiments of the present invention, those skilled in the art will realize that many
variations and modifications may be made to affect the described invention. Many of
those variations and modifications will provide the same result and fall within the spirit of
the claimed invention. It is the intention, therefore, to limit the invention only as
indicated by the scope of the claims.

Within each group other than argument, or within each argument issue type, distribute the budget among applicable criteria in proportion to each criterion's relative_weight. Use unrounded weights throughout the calculation.
weight_allocation.final_score: round(100 * C, 1), only when every applicable criterion is scored
weight_allocation.baseline_warning: The all-applicable percentages are illustrative only. Do not drop inapplicable entries from those percentages and renormalize the resulting flat list.
weight_allocation.calibration_note: These weights are initial design values, not proportions prescribed by the Word standard, and have not yet been calibrated against the new 100-case set.

applicability.amendment_rule: G3-G5 activate together when the candidate actually amends the claims and are scored using the Word levels. If the synchronized zero-score rule applies, all three remain active with score 0. Otherwise, when no amendment is made, all three are not_applicable.
applicability.argument_rule: Determine applicability of each G6 criterion from the complete OA, the actual points of dispute, the jurisdiction, and the necessary reasoning steps. A single inventive-step objection may require several subcriteria. A missing candidate response does not make an existing issue not applicable.
applicability.not_applicable: Use status=not_applicable and score=null only when a conditional criterion does not apply; provide the reason and references to source materials. Only not_applicable releases allocated weight.

amendment_zero_rule.trigger: The Judge determines that the claims should be amended, but the candidate OAR has not chosen an amendment strategy.
amendment_zero_rule.evidence_requirement: Each of G3-G5 must cite the case basis showing why amendment is needed and evidence that the candidate did not choose that strategy. A difference between pre_claim and post_claim alone is insufficient to infer that amendment is required.
amendment_zero_rule.defect_description_requirement: Each criterion's defect description must identify its current metric ID and explain that the zero score is required by this synchronized rule.
amendment_zero_rule.scope: Do not mark these three criteria not_applicable or redistribute the amendment budget. G2, G6, and all other scoring rules continue to apply as specified.

result_contract.scored: A score of 0, 0.5, or 1 and verifiable evidence references are required.
result_contract.unscored: not_applicable, not_evaluable, and failed require score=null. Conditional not_applicable results require a reason and source references.
result_contract.failure_handling: not_evaluable and failed retain their allocated shares and block the final score. Do not redistribute their shares to scored criteria or remove an inventive-step type because one subcriterion cannot be evaluated.
result_contract.consistency_checks: Validate required criteria, consistent applicability of G3-G5, compliance with the synchronized zero-score rule, and evidence fields. Programmatic checks do not replace semantic review.

audit_fields.common_group_allocation: Group budgets, active criteria, and argument.types with issue-type budgets and subcriteria.
audit_fields.common_allocated_weights: Allocated weights including shares reserved for not_evaluable or failed criteria.
audit_fields.common_effective_weights: Weights actually contributing to the score; not_applicable, not_evaluable, and failed have effective weight 0. Failed or unevaluable applicable criteria still block a final total.

scoring_policy.duplicate_defect_rule: Assign each minimal defect to one primary criterion rather than penalizing it repeatedly across criteria. The explicitly required synchronized G3-G5 zero scores are a policy exception; each must identify the current criterion and the reason for the rule-based zero score.

metrics.name: Accuracy of understanding the case facts and Office Action
metrics.evaluation_object: Whether the application, its current claims, the Office Action, and the relevant cited documents are correctly understood, and whether the validity of the grounds for objection is correctly assessed.

levels.1: Correctly understands the application, the claims, the technical features, and their relationships; accurately understands the meaning of the grounds for objection and accurately assesses whether they are valid.
levels.0.5: Correctly assesses the main technical solution, the grounds for objection, and the points open to argument, but has localized misunderstandings of noncritical facts, feature relationships, or document content; these do not change the main direction of the response and can be corrected locally.
levels.0: Misunderstands the technical solution of the application, feature relationships, or the Office Action; makes errors such as confusing the original claims, the current claims, and the proposed amended claims.

metrics.activation_condition: Required for every case.

metrics.name: Reasonableness of the overall response strategy
metrics.evaluation_object: Whether the choice between relying solely on argument and proactively amending the claims is reasonable; if proactive amendment is chosen, whether the choice of claims to amend is reasonable and whether any improper admissions are made.

levels.1: The choice of argument alone, amendment, or a combination of the two is supported by the case; the claims selected for treatment are appropriate, and the overall strategy addresses the core issues in the Office Action; no unsupported, materially adverse admissions are made.
levels.0.5: The main response approach is reasonable, but there are localized inappropriate choices in the treatment of noncore claims that do not affect the main position.
levels.0: The main response approach cannot address the core issues, for example, persisting with argument alone when the arguments lack a valid basis, or failing to include core claims requiring amendment in the strategy; makes adverse admissions that lack a basis in the Office Action and materially weaken the position on the main scope of protection.

metrics.activation_condition: Required for every case.

metrics.name: Effectiveness of claim amendments in addressing the issues identified in the Office Action [if amended]
metrics.evaluation_object: Whether the claim amendments themselves resolve the issues targeted by the Office Action, assessed separately from the quality of the response statement.

levels.1: The specific amendments correspond to the issues identified in the Office Action, and the amended claims, together with the response statement, are sufficient to overcome those defects.
levels.0.5: The amendments resolve the core defects identified in the Office Action, but the treatment of noncore defects is incomplete and requires localized correction.
levels.0: The core defects identified in the Office Action remain after amendment; or the amendments have no substantive connection to the defects identified in the Office Action.

metrics.name: Proportionality of claim amendments and preservation of the scope of protection [if amended]
metrics.evaluation_object: Whether there is avoidable loss of protection while reasonably addressing the Office Action, assessed against the original protection objectives of the case.

levels.1: Added limitations, claim deletions, and other scope adjustments are reasonably necessary or reflect supported strategic tradeoffs; there is no unnecessary narrowing that can be clearly demonstrated from the case materials.
levels.0.5: There are individual unnecessary additional limitations or losses of noncore claims, but the main protection objectives of the original application are not materially affected; a less restrictive and equally reasonable localized adjustment can be specifically identified.
levels.0: Despite the existence of a supported, reasonable approach involving less narrowing, introduces significantly unnecessary limitations, deletes important claims, or abandons key protected subject matter, materially harming the main protection objectives.

metrics.name: Legality and formal compliance of claim amendments [if amended]
metrics.evaluation_object: Whether amendments have a basis in the original disclosure and comply with amendment rules; whether clarity, support, antecedent basis, and claim dependencies meet the applicable requirements.

levels.1: The amended claim content and combinations have a verifiable basis in the original disclosure and comply with the applicable amendment rules; the amended claims are clear and supported by the description, with correct terminology, antecedent basis, and claim dependencies.
levels.0.5: The amendments have a basis in the original disclosure and the scope of protection can be determined, but there are correctable localized wording or citation-form defects; correction does not change the substantive technical solution.
levels.0: The amendments exceed the permissible scope, introduce content or combinations lacking a basis in the original disclosure, or create generalizations unsupported by the description; substantive errors in key wording, feature relationships, or claim dependencies make the scope of protection indeterminate or the technical solution untenable.

metrics.name: Quality of analysis of the closest prior art and distinguishing technical features

levels.1: Accepts or challenges the examiner's identification of the closest prior art on a supported basis; correctly identifies the specific differences between the claims and the closest prior art, correctly analyzes and defines the distinguishing technical features, and clearly and sufficiently performs the feature comparison needed to support that conclusion.
levels.0.5: Correctly identifies the closest prior art and the main distinguishing technical features, but some comparisons, feature relationships, or explanations of the supporting basis are incomplete; these can be supplemented using the existing materials.
levels.0: The identification of distinguishing technical features is untenable, or distinguishing technical features decisive to the conclusion are omitted; rejects the starting point for comparison without a basis; merely asserts that "differences exist" without substantively comparing the features at the core of the dispute.

metrics.name: Quality of analysis of the technical effects of the distinguishing technical features and the technical problem actually solved

levels.1: Uses the description, appropriate evidence, or reasonable technical analysis to explain how the distinguishing features and their interaction produce the relevant technical effects; accurately defines the technical problem actually solved on that basis; accurately assesses whether the examiner has incorporated the means of solving the problem disclosed in the application into the definition of the technical problem, and reasonably addresses disagreements with the examiner's definition of that problem.
levels.0.5: The main assessment of the technical effects of the distinguishing technical features and the technical problem actually solved is supported, but the explanation of the causal relationship between features and effects, or of the relationship between the effects achieved by the distinguishing technical features in the invention and the technical problem actually solved, is insufficient; the main argument can be completed by elaborating on the existing basis.
levels.0: Incorrectly defines the technical effects that the distinguishing technical features can achieve in the invention or the technical problem actually solved, or misunderstands or reasons incorrectly about the derivation connecting the two, resulting in an incorrect key foundation for the inventive step response.

metrics.name: Quality of analysis and rebuttal concerning other cited documents and common general knowledge

levels.1: For cited documents or common general knowledge used to supply the distinguishing technical features, accurately analyzes their disclosed content, the functions of their features, and the differences from the distinguishing technical features of the application; acceptance or challenge of a finding of common general knowledge is consistent with the evidence and applicable rules on the burden of proof.
levels.0.5: Correctly assesses the functions of features in other cited documents and the direction of the rebuttal, but inadequately analyzes localized correspondences or the basis for the finding of common general knowledge.
levels.0: The substantive analysis of content used to supply key distinguishing technical features is incorrect, or the main differences relied on for rebuttal are untenable; merely asserts that something is "not disclosed" or "not common general knowledge," without the explanation or evidence needed to support the core conclusion.

levels.1: Addresses the examiner's actual reasons for combination and, in light of the technical effects of the distinguishing technical features and the actual technical problem, sufficiently analyzes the motivation to modify, technical teachings, conditions for combination, or barriers to combination, reaching a correctly supported conclusion on whether the overall claimed solution is obvious; explicitly checks whether the cited documents are compatible in their technical environments, operating principles, functions, and cooperative relationships; accurately identifies whether the examiner has used the application as a roadmap to reconstruct a combination of prior art.
levels.0.5: Provides effective analysis directly relevant to the reasons for combination, but inadequately explains some combination steps, functional relationships, or barriers to combination; the main direction of the argument is valid.
levels.0: Fails to effectively address the reasons for combination that determine the examination conclusion; asserts that combination is impossible solely because of differences in technical fields, technical problems, or effects; or fails to clearly explain why a person skilled in the art could not arrive at the overall claimed solution by following the stated reasons.

metrics.notes: The "four samenesses" are not a mandatory structure requiring rebuttal of each element.

levels.1: Addresses the novelty objection by analyzing the claims and relevant cited documents under the applicable principle of comparison with each reference separately, identifying differences that affect the novelty determination and their supporting basis; where amendments are used, explains why the amended solution is not fully disclosed by the cited content.
levels.0.5: Identifies supported substantive technical differences, but inadequately explains feature correspondences, disclosed content, or the significance of the differences; the argument can be completed by elaborating on the existing materials.
levels.0: Fails to develop a substantive argument capable of supporting novelty; the main reasons concern only superficial differences in use, technical field, problem, or effect and cannot explain substantive differences in the technical solution; or relies on untenable feature differences to support the conclusion.

levels.1: Provides a supported analysis of the specific grounds for subject-matter exclusion in relation to the solution defined by the claims, sufficiently explaining why the original or amended solution satisfies the corresponding subject-matter requirements.
levels.0.5: The direction of the subject-matter assessment is correct and the specific solution is discussed, but some elements or relationships decisive to that assessment are insufficiently explained.
levels.0: Fails to substantively address the specific grounds for exclusion; substitutes labels such as "involves technology" or "uses a computer" for the necessary analysis; or the stated reasons cannot support a conclusion that the solution satisfies the applicable subject-matter requirements.

levels.1: Accurately distinguishes the disclosure or description defects actually identified in the OA and, using the original application documents and knowledge or evidence that may lawfully be relied on, sufficiently explains that the corresponding requirements are satisfied or how a lawful adjustment addresses the defect.
levels.0.5: Identifies original content or evidence directly relevant to the defect and takes the correct direction in the response, but inadequately explains the implementation path, the correspondence to the description, or the extent of support.
levels.0: Fails to explain the core implementation or description obstacle identified; merely asserts that the subject matter "has already been disclosed"; substitutes new content incapable of remedying the original defect for the required disclosure, or relies on reasons unrelated to the actual defect to support the conclusion.

levels.1: Accurately locates the identified problem with feature descriptions, protection boundaries, support for generalization, or claim form, and sufficiently addresses the corresponding defect through supported explanations or explanations of amendments.
levels.0.5: Provides an explanation or explanation of amendments that addresses the specific problem in the correct direction, but the correspondence or reasons for compliance are incomplete.
levels.0: Fails to substantively explain the specific defect; merely asserts in general terms that the claims are "clear," "supported," or "compliant"; or the argument fails to explain why the core ambiguity, support gap, or formal error has been addressed.

levels.1: Accurately explains the technical problem being solved, the essential features, and their functional relationships, and uses the original disclosure to sufficiently demonstrate that the existing independent claim defines a complete solution or to explain how adding the relevant features completes that solution.
levels.0.5: The main assessment of the technical problem and essential features is correct, but the explanation of why the existing features are sufficient, why the added features are necessary, or how the features function together is insufficient.
levels.0: Fails to substantively analyze necessity; incorrectly treats optional features as essential or essential features as optional and bases the main conclusion on that error; the core argument cannot explain how the independent claim defines a complete solution to the stated technical problem.

metrics.name: Logical coherence of the overall argument
metrics.evaluation_object: Connections and consistency across paragraphs, claims, and different grounds of argument; the quality of reasoning on an individual point of dispute falls primarily under item 6.

levels.1: The main arguments, evidence, and conclusions throughout the text are clearly connected, the logical chain is complete, and the different grounds of argument are mutually coherent; the response statement is consistent with the final claims.
levels.0.5: The main positions and conclusions are consistent, but there are noncritical gaps in logical connections, repetitions, or localized inconsistencies in wording; the intended meaning can be clearly determined from context.
levels.0: Core arguments or factual premises conflict and cannot hold simultaneously, or the logical chain is incomplete or contains gaps; the main conclusion contradicts the evidence presented; key limitations relied on in the response statement are absent from the final claims being pursued, causing a mismatch in the subject of the main argument.

metrics.name: Completeness of the response to the Office Action
metrics.evaluation_object: Whether all issues mentioned in the response statement have been addressed, without reassessing the sufficiency of responses already made.

levels.1: All Office Action objections, affected claims, and independent points of dispute requiring treatment are explicitly addressed; the scope of consolidated responses, amendments, deletions, or reliance on common reasons is clear, with no omissions.
levels.0.5: All core issues are addressed, but noncore objections or secondary issues affecting noncore claims are omitted.
levels.0: The response omits a major type of Office Action objection, so that the response as a whole fails to cover the main issues that must be resolved in this round; merely naming an issue without providing any treatment does not count as addressing it.

metrics.name: Completeness of deliverables and conformity with textual conventions
metrics.notes: This item combines four checks: required documents; numbering and versions; terminology and written expression; formatting and grammar. Terminology errors here concern expression and word choice; actual misunderstandings of technical concepts fall under item 1, and substantive conflicts in position fall under item 7.

levels.1: All documents required by the task are provided, including the required amended text and comparison materials where amendments are actually made; requests, claims, cited documents, figures, application numbers, and versions are correctly numbered and matched; terminology is standard and consistent, expression is professional, clear, and concise, grammar, wording, hierarchy, and punctuation follow conventions, and no unresolved placeholders remain.
levels.0.5: All required documents are provided, and the final text for submission and the objects cited can be uniquely identified, but there are localized numbering typos, inconsistent terminology, mildly colloquial language, redundancy, typographical errors, ungrammatical sentences, or formatting problems; these do not change the technical meaning, requests, or reference targets and can be corrected locally.
levels.0: A required document is missing; the final claim version, request, or key reference target cannot be determined; unfilled placeholders remain in key locations; or problems with language, terminology, numbering, or layout prevent accurate understanding of the main content or require substantial rewriting.

metrics.name: Compliance with the applicable jurisdiction and examination rules
metrics.evaluation_object: Whether the legal assessment standards, response logic, amendment principles, and procedural rules used in the response apply under the laws and regulations of the country corresponding to the case.

levels.1: The assessment standards, response logic, amendment principles, and procedural treatment actually used are consistent with the jurisdiction, procedural stage, and applicable version of the law for the case; where legal authorities are cited, their content and scope of application are correct.
levels.0.5: The substantive assessment standards and procedural treatment are correct, but there are isolated errors in statutory provision numbers, names of laws, version labels, or legal terminology; correcting them does not change the assessment standards, response conclusions, or procedural validity.
levels.0: Applies substantive rules from an inapplicable jurisdiction, procedural stage, or version of the law; misunderstands key legal requirements, examination rules, or procedural restrictions, making the main grounds of response, amendment principles, or procedural treatment untenable.

metrics.name: Authenticity of factual statements and citations [hallucination control]
metrics.evaluation_object: Whether the response asserts the existence of content, facts, data, Office Action objections, or sources that do not actually exist. Supported technical inferences, explicitly labeled assumptions, and proactive analysis of genuine issues not mentioned in the OA are not hallucinations. Misinterpretation of real content falls primarily under item 1.

levels.1: Factual statements and citations can be verified from the corresponding materials or real sources; citations support the stated views, and reasonable inferences are distinguished from the original disclosure and established facts; no Office Action objections, technical content, data, or sources are fabricated, and no nonexistent Office Action objections are answered.
levels.0.5: No facts or sources are fabricated, but the scope of support from individual real sources is overstated; narrowing the statement corrects the problem, and the relevant conclusion remains sufficiently supported by the real grounds already identified.
levels.0: Fabricates application content, cited-document content, experimental data, facts, Office Action objections, or citation sources, or answers nonexistent Office Action objections.

metrics.activation_condition: Required for every case.
