PTOL-326 (Rev. 03-11) | Office Action Summary | Part of Paper No./Mail Date 20120725 | | :--- | :--- | :--- | Application/Control Number: 12/890,234 Art Unit: 2853 Page 2 ### DETAILED ACTION #### *Election/Restrictions* 1. Applicant's election without traverse of Group II, claims 7-19 in the reply filed on 6/29/2012 is acknowledged. 2. Claims 1-6 are withdrawn from further consideration pursuant to 37 CFR 1.142(b) as being drawn to a nonelected invention there being no allowable generic or linking claim. Election was made **without** traverse in the reply filed on 6/29/2012. #### *Information Disclosure Statement* 3. The information disclosure statement (IDS) submitted on 9/24/2010 is in compliance with the provisions of 37 CFR 1.97. Accordingly, the information disclosure statement is being considered by the examiner. #### *Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 112* 4. The following is a quotation of the second paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 112: > The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the applicant regards as his invention. 5. Claims 7-19 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which applicant regards as the invention. In claim 7, line 8 the recitation of "each actuator in each array of actuators" has no antecedent basis. In claims 14 and 19, line 2 the recitation of "the top surfaces of the walls" has no antecedent basis. Application/Control Number: 12/890,234 Art Unit: 2853 Page 3 In claim 15, it is not clearly understood what the difference is between "a flexible member" recited in line 6 and "a membrane" recited in line 9. #### *Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 102* 6. The following is a quotation of the appropriate paragraphs of 35 U.S.C. 102 that form the basis for the rejections under this section made in this Office action: > A person shall be entitled to a patent unless - > (b) the invention was patented or described in a printed publication in this or a foreign country or in public use or on sale in this country, more than one year prior to the date of application for patent in the United States. 7. Claims 7-9 and 11 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(b) as being anticipated by Barnes et al. (US 7,254,890 B2). Barnes et al. discloses a multi-layered structure (Fig. 4A) suitable for use in manufacturing inkjet printheads comprising: **1)** a wafer (34) including a plurality of die sites (14) arranged in a predetermined pattern (col 5, lns 9-10), a polymer layer (46) including a plurality of apertures (52) arrays arranged in a predetermined pattern corresponding to the predetermined pattern of the plurality of die sites (14) on the wafer, the polymer layer (46) and wafer being bonded together to enable each actuator (heater resistors 36) in each array of actuators formed in each die site (14) on the wafer (34) to be aligned with an aperture (52) in a corresponding aperture array formed in the polymer layer (46) (col 5, lns 27-31; col 6, lns 29-36), **2)** wherein each actuator (36) in each array of actuators is positioned to urge ink through a corresponding aperture (52) in each array of apertures (as shown in Fig. 4B), **3)** the wafer (34) being primarily composed of silicon (col 5, lns 27-28), and **4)** an inter-die region that separates the die Application/Control Number: 12/890,234 Art Unit: 2853 Page 4 sites (14) in the plurality of die sites on the wafer (34) from one another; and a corresponding region that separates the aperture arrays in the plurality of aperture arrays in the polymer layer from one another (well known). Barnes et al. further at least teaches that actuators may be piezoelectric devices or heater resistors (col 5, lns 27-30) #### *Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103* 8. The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103(a) which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action: > (a) A patent may not be obtained though the invention is not identically disclosed or described as set forth in section 102 of this title, if the differences between the subject matter sought to be patented and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which said subject matter pertains. Patentability shall not be negatived by the manner in which the invention was made. 9. Claims 10 and 12-19 rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Barnes et al. (US 7,254,890 B2) in view of Shingyohuchi (US 6,811,238 B2). Barnes et al. discloses a multi-layered structure (Fig. 4A) suitable for use in manufacturing inkjet printheads comprising: **1)** a wafer (34) including a plurality of die sites (14) arranged in a predetermined pattern (col 5, lns 9-10), a polymer layer (46) including a plurality of apertures (52) arrays arranged in a predetermined pattern corresponding to the predetermined pattern of the plurality of die sites (14) on the wafer, the polymer layer (46) and wafer being bonded together to enable each actuator (36) in each array of actuators formed in each die site (14) on the wafer (34) to be aligned with an aperture (52) in a corresponding aperture array formed in the polymer layer (46) (col 5, lns 27-31; col 6, lns 29-36), **2)** wherein each actuator (36) in each array of actuators is positioned to urge ink through a corresponding aperture (52) in each array of Application/Control Number: 12/890,234 Art Unit: 2853 Page 5 apertures (as shown in Fig. 4B), **3)** the wafer (34) being primarily composed of silicon (col 5, lns 27-28), **4)** an inter-die region that separates the die sites (14) in the plurality of die sites on the wafer (34) from one another; and a corresponding region that separates the aperture arrays in the plurality of aperture arrays in the polymer layer from one another (well known), and **5)** a polymer layer (46) including a plurality of aperture arrays arranged in a predetermined pattern corresponding to the predetermined pattern of the plurality of die sites (14) on the wafer (34), each aperture array on the polymer layer having a plurality of apertures (52) with each aperture placed in fluid communication with a corresponding fluid chamber (48) in each die site on the wafer, and the polymer layer and wafer being bonded together (col 6, lns 31-36 as shown in Fig. 4A). Barnes et al. further at least teaches that actuators may be piezoelectric devices or heater resistors (col 5, lns 27-30). Barnes et al. does not teach **1)** each actuator further comprising a region of polysilicon on the wafer, **2)** an array of actuators formed on a surface of each die site on the wafer, each actuator having a flexible membrane, and a plurality of walls extending from the surface of each die site on the wafer to a position above the flexible membranes, the walls and flexible membranes forming a plurality of fluid cavities, with a fluid cavity positioned over each actuator in each of the arrays of actuators, **3)** wherein the polymer layer is bonded to top surface of the walls, **4)** an adhesive layer positioned between the top surfaces of the walls and the polymer layer, **5)** an array of fluid chambers positioned over each array of actuators in each die site on the wafer, each fluid chamber in the array of fluid chambers being formed above a membrane in the Application/Control Number: 12/890,234 Art Unit: 2853 Page 6 array of actuators. Shingyohuchi at least teaches each actuator further comprising a region of polysilicon on the wafer (well known), an array of actuators (diaphragm 50/electrode 55) formed on a surface of each die site (42) on the wafer, each actuator having a flexible membrane (diaphragm 50) (col 8, lns 52-57), and a plurality of walls (formed by 41) extending from the surface of each die site on the wafer to a position above the flexible membranes (50), the walls (41) and flexible membranes forming a plurality of fluid cavities (gap 56), with a fluid cavity (56) positioned over each actuator (50/55) in each of the arrays of actuators (col 8, lns 52-57 as shown in Fig. 5), wherein the polymer layer (nozzle plate 43) is bonded to top surface of the walls (41) (as shown in Fig. 5), an adhesive layer positioned between the top surfaces of the walls and the polymer layer (43) (col 9, lns 54-55), an array of fluid chambers (46) positioned over each array of actuators (50/55) in each die site (42) on the wafer, each fluid chamber (46) in the array of fluid chambers being formed above a membrane in the array of actuators (col 8, lns 5-12, lns 51-57). It would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having ordinary skill in the inkjet art to substitute the micro ejection head utilizing heater resistor actuators of Barnes et al. with the ink jet head utilizing piezoelectric actuators as taught to be old by Shingyohuchi for the purpose of ejecting ink droplets of a considerable size and a finer size with respect to a nozzle diameter. #### *Conclusion* 10. field_values.desc:
# Description

TECHNICAL FIELD

[0001] This disclosure relates generally to methods for manufacturing components used in inkjet printheads, and more particularly, to methods for fabricating composite layers used in inkjet printheads.
BACKGROUND

[0002] Micro-electromechanical systems (MEMS) are mechanical systems that are micromachined in silicon and may be optionally integrated with control electronic circuits. MEMS are generally categorized as either microsensor or microactuator systems, depending on the application. MEMS incorporate electrostatic, electromagnetic, thermoelastic, piezoelectric, or piezoresistive effects in the operations of the systems.

[0003] One use for MEMS devices is in drop on demand inkjet technology that has been employed in commercial products, such as printers, plotters, and facsimile machines. Generally, an inkjet image is formed by the selective activation of inkjets within a printhead to eject ink onto an ink receiving member. To facilitate manufacture of an inkjet array printhead, an array of inkjet ejectors can be formed from multiple laminated plates or sheets. These sheets are configured with arrays of ink droplet ejectors. Each ejector may include structures such as an actuator, pressure chamber, outlet, and aperture nozzle. These structures are formed from the superposition of the multiple laminated structural layers. An example of a laminated layer inkjet array for a printhead includes a silicon layer bonded to an aperture layer formed on a polymer material, such as polyimide or thermoplastic. The silicon layer includes an array of actuators. Each actuator has an associated ink inlet, diaphragm, and pressure chamber area. The polymer aperture layer includes an aperture in the form of a nozzle. Walls are formed on the silicon layer to for a pressure chamber for each operator and the polymer aperture layer is bonded to the walls to enclose the pressure chamber and establish fluid communication between each aperture in the aperture layer and each pressure chamber formed on the silicon layer. Once formed, each actuator in the array of actuators may be selectively activated to deform the diaphragm and expel an ink droplet from the pressure chamber through the aperture.

[0004] The process for bonding the polymer aperture plate to the walls extending from the silicon layer requires alignment of the apertures in the aperture layer with the silicon layer. Existing manufacturing processes produce actuator arrays by forming a plurality of actuator arrays on a silicon wafer and then cutting the silicon wafer to separate the actuator arrays from one another. The inlets, diaphragms, and walls are then formed on the actuator arrays and the polymer aperture plate is bonded to the walls extending from the silicon plate. Known methods of aligning apertures in an aperture plate to actuators and their associated structure on the silicon layer often result in alignment errors of at least five microns in magnitude. Increased efficiencies and improved precision in alignment in the manufacture of the MEMS printheads would be beneficial to the fields of imaging in general, and inkjet printing in particular.
SUMMARY

[0005] An improved method for manufacturing components useful for inkjet printheads has been developed. The method includes forming a plurality of die sites on a wafer in a predetermined pattern, forming a plurality of aperture arrays on a polymer layer, aligning the die sites on the wafer with the aperture arrays on the polymer layer, bonding the wafer and the polymer layer together; and cutting the bonded wafer and the polymer layer to form a plurality of bonded dies. Each die site includes an array of inkjet actuators and each aperture array includes a plurality of apertures. The plurality of aperture arrays are arranged in a pattern corresponding to the predetermined pattern of the die sites on the wafer and the polymer layer has a size and a shape corresponding to a size and a shape of the wafer.

[0006] In at lease one embodiment, a multi-layered structure suitable for use in manufacturing inkjet printheads includes a wafer having a plurality of die sites arranged in a predetermined pattern, and a polymer layer that includes a plurality of aperture arrays arranged in a predetermined pattern corresponding to the predetermined pattern of the plurality of die sites on the wafer. The polymer layer and wafer are bonded together to enable each actuator in each array of actuators formed in each die site on the wafer to be aligned with an aperture in a corresponding aperture array formed in the polymer layer.

[0007] In at least another embodiment, a multi-layered structure suitable for use in manufacturing inkjet printheads includes a wafer having a plurality of die sites arranged in a predetermined pattern, an array of actuators arranged on a surface of each die site of the wafer, an array of fluid chambers positioned over each array of actuators in each die site on the wafer, and a polymer layer including a plurality of aperture arrays arranged in a predetermined pattern corresponding to the predetermined pattern of the plurality of die sites on the wafer. Each actuator in each array of actuators includes a flexible membrane. Each fluid chamber in the array of fluid chambers is formed above a membrane in the array of actuators. Each aperture array on the polymer layer has a plurality of apertures with each aperture placed in fluid communication with a corresponding fluid chamber in each die site on the wafer, and the polymer layer and wafer are bonded together.
BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE DRAWINGS

[0008] FIG. 1A is an illustration of a wafer having multiple die sites.

[0009] FIG. 1B is a more detailed view of two die sites in the wafer of FIG. 1A, each die site having an actuator array and a pressure chamber formed over each actuator in the array.

[0010] FIG. 1C is an illustration of a polymer film having multiple aperture arrays.

[0011] FIG. 1D is a more detailed view of two aperture arrays formed in the polymer film of FIG. 1C.

[0012] FIG. 2 is a cross-sectional view of a polymer layer showing two of the apertures in one aperture array.

[0013] FIG. 3 is a flow diagram of a batch process for producing multiple dies, each die having an actuator array and aligned apertures.

[0014] FIG. 4A is a perspective view of the polymer layer of FIG. 1C bonded to the silicon wafer of FIG. 1A.

[0015] FIG. 4B is a perspective view of the bonded wafer and polymer layer of FIG. 4A separated into multiple dies.

[0016] FIG. 5 is a plan view of two inkjet ejector arrays formed in a wafer.

[0017] FIG. 6 is a cross-sectional view of an inkjet ejector on one die along the cross-sectional lines for FIG. 6 shown in FIG. 5.
DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE DRAWINGS

[0018] The description below and the accompanying figures provide a general understanding of the environment for the system and method disclosed herein as well as the details for the system and method. In the drawings, like reference numerals are used throughout to designate like elements. As used herein, the term “wafer” refers to a planar material sheet adapted to have multiple repeated instances of a structural pattern formed on and through the surface of the wafer. A common example of a wafer is a silicon wafer used in the fabrication of microelectronics and micro electro-mechanical system (MEMS) devices. Common examples of these wafers have approximately circular shapes with diameters between 25 mm and 450 mm and thicknesses of approximately 275 μm to 950 μm. While the wafer is often primarily composed of a silicon substrate, wafers may also include planar layers of other materials, such as metals. Selected regions of a wafer may include chemicals diffused into the wafer substrate in a process known as doping. While wafers with silicon substrates are widely used in industry, other materials, including metallic crystals formed from elements of the III-V group in the periodic table, may also be used to form wafers. A photoresist material, which is typically a polymeric material, may optionally cover a wafer substrate. A positive photoresist material becomes soluble to chemical solvents in response to exposure to radiation. A negative photoresist material becomes insoluble to chemical solvents once exposed to radiation, typically actinic radiation. One example of a negative photoresist commonly used in microfluidic applications is SU-8, a polymer that may coat a wafer in thicknesses ranging between about 0.1 micrometers and 2 millimeters. As used herein, a “microfluidic structure” may refer to a variety of channels, passageways, openings, or chambers formed in one or more layers of material adapted to transport and hold a quantity of fluid such as ink. Typical microfluidic structures have dimensions ranging from about 500 microns to less than 1 micron in size. Photolithographic techniques may be used to pattern and etch structures, such as microfluidic channels and chambers, into photoresist materials as well as the underlying wafer. Various deposition techniques including vapor deposition, sputtering, spin coating, plating, and other techniques known to the art may also form structures, including microfluidic channels and chambers, on the surface of the underlying wafer. As used herein, the term “die site” refers to a defined section disposed within a larger layer of material. The layer is typically a wafer, and each die site contains one or more structures that remain intact after a die site is cut from the layer. A plurality of die sites are formed on a wafer, and each die site includes one instance of a structural pattern formed on the wafer. A wafer is typically formed with a plurality of die sites arranged in a pattern, such as a two dimensional grid. An inter-die region separates the die sites to enable cutting of each die site from the layer without damaging the structures in the die site. Die sites often have rectangular shapes with the same structure repeated in each die site on a layer in many common embodiments.

[0019] A wafer 104 having multiple die sites that are arranged in a grid pattern is shown in FIG. 1A. Two die sites 108A and 108B are shown in the magnified view of FIG. 1B. Each die site includes ten actuators 112 having open pressure chambers formed over them. The actuators and pressure chambers are arranged in an array having two rows with each row having five actuators and pressure chambers. An ink inlet 128 that is etched through the wafer 104 in each die site enables an external fluid source to be coupled to the pressure chambers. Inter-die region 110 separates die site 108A from die site 108B. The remaining die sites are similarly separated. Thus, cutting through the inter-die regions 110 of the wafer 104 separates the die sites from one another. Each separated piece of the wafer that contains an actuator array is called a die, and the cutting process may be referred to as “dicing” the wafer. While not a requirement, die sites on a wafer typically have uniform dimensions, and each die site contains a single actuator array structure similar to the ones contained in the other die sites. The predetermined pattern used to arrange the die sites is typically a two-dimensional grid, although alternative die site patterns may be used.

[0020] Various techniques known to the art may be used to form the actuator arrays and pressure chambers at the die sites shown in FIG. 1A and FIG. 1B. Multiple iterations of material depositions, patterning operations, and etching processes may be performed to form an actuator array and pressure chamber at each die site of the wafer 104. The techniques used to implement these depositions, operations, and processes are well known. The microfluidic structures formed on the wafer may be made with photoresist materials, metallic depositions, and other materials applied to the wafer. The structures formed by these materials and techniques include channels that enable fluid to flow through the microfluidic structures, walls that form cavities for pressure chambers, and openings that enable fluid to enter the wafer from an external source. Electrostatic actuators, electromechanical actuators, such as piezoelectric elements, or thermal actuators may be mounted to the surface of the silicon wafer. The plurality of actuator arrays and microfluidic structures of each die site are arranged in a predefined pattern to form a portion of a printhead to be used in an inkjet printer.

[0021] A polymer layer 116 that has been prepared for bonding to the wafer 104 to cover the microfluidic structures constructed on the layer is shown in FIG. 1C. The polymer film is typically a plate or a sheet of a polymer, such as a polyimide or thermoplastic, cut to approximately the same shape and size as the wafer 104. The polymer film may include a single layer, or multiple layers that incorporate adhesive layers for bonding with the wafer, and an optional anti-wetting coating on an outward facing surface of the polymer film. Polymer film layer 116 has a size and shape corresponding to wafer 104. A plurality of aperture arrays are arranged in a grid pattern that corresponds to the die site grid pattern in wafer 104. FIG. 1D shows a magnified view of two aperture arrays 124A and 124B in polymer film 116. Each aperture array includes ten apertures 136 that are arranged in two rows with each row having five apertures. Region 132 separates the aperture array 108A from aperture array 108B. The remaining aperture arrays are similarly separated. Each aperture array is positioned at a location that corresponds to an actuator array die site in wafer 104.

[0022] The apertures are formed in the polymer layer 116 using various techniques, which include laser ablation. An example of a laser ablation technique includes ablating an aperture in the layer 116 with an excimer laser. A cross-sectional view of the layer 116 is shown in FIG. 2. In the example embodiment of FIG. 2, an excimer laser ablates apertures from the bonding surface 212 towards the exterior surface 216 as indicated by arrow 220. The laser is controlled in a known manner to form a plurality of aperture arrays having apertures 136 with the tapered shape depicted in FIG. 2. The surface 212 of layer 116 is configured to bond to the structures on the wafer that form the pressure chambers. Surface 216 of the layer 116 has been covered with an antiwetting coating 206 that is deposited on polymer layer 116 prior to ablation of the layer to form the apertures. The antiwetting coating 206 resists adhesion of ink to the exposed surface of the aperture layer during printing operations.

[0023] FIG. 3 depicts a process 300 that forms multiple dies for the manufacture of inkjet printheads. Process 300 begins with the construction of microfluidic structure on a silicon wafer (block 304) and the formation of the apertures in the aperture arrays on the polymer layer (block 308). The die sites one the wafer are then aligned with the aperture arrays on the polymer film (block 312). The alignment may be facilitated with alignment features that were formed in the circumference of the wafer and the polymer layer during the processes performed in blocks 304 and 308. The alignment process places each aperture in the polymer film layer in fluid communication with a corresponding pressure chamber on the wafer. Following the alignment, the polymer layer is bonded to the wafer (block 316). After the bonding process is completed, the bonded wafer and polymer layer may be cut, or diced, into individual actuator array and aperture plate dies (block 320).

[0024] The bonding of the wafer and the polymer layer may be achieved with a thin layer of epoxy interposed between the polymer layer and bonding surfaces on the wafer. A suitable epoxy for the bonding process includes Epon® epoxy, as well as alternative adhesives including phenolic, polyimide, and acrylic adhesive layers. The example bonding process includes the application of heat and pressure to the wafer and polymer film layers. The heat and pressure may cause an uneven thermal expansion between the wafer and the polymer layer. This uneven expansion may place stress on the wafer and cause the wafer to crack. To address this uneven expansion and reduce the risk of wafer cracking, gaps, such as the gap 120 shown in FIG. 1D, may be included in the layer 116 to separate the aperture arrays in the polymer layer. The gaps provide an area between each aperture array where the polymer layer may expand while reducing stress applied to the wafer.

[0025] After the wafer and the polymer film have been bonded together, they form a multi-layered composite wafer such as the composite wafer 404 shown in FIG. 4A. In that figure, the polymer film 116 has been aligned and bonded to the underlying silicon wafer 104. Each aperture array in the polymer film 116 is adequately aligned with a corresponding pressure chamber in a die site in the wafer 104 to enable each aperture in the polymer layer to be in fluid communication with a pressure chamber overlying an actuator in an actuator array at each die site on the wafer 404. This bonded composite wafer may then be cut along the inter-die regions of the wafer 104 to form the bonded dies 432 shown in FIG. 4B. Typical dicing methods include cutting along the inter-die regions with a mechanical saw or a laser cutter. Thus, the process of FIG. 3 is an efficient method for manufacturing dies for inkjet printheads. The process 300 may produce bonded dies 432 having alignment errors between each aperture and pressure chamber of less than one micron in magnitude.

[0026] A portion of the bonded composite wafer 404 is shown in FIG. 5. Each aperture 136 (shown in phantom in the figure) is aligned with a pressure chamber, such as 530A, that overlies an actuator 524 in an actuator array. The inter-die region 510 separates one bonded die site 508A from the other bonded die site 508B. In the example of FIG. 5, a microfluidic channel 532 in wafer 404 enables fluid communication between the inlet 128 and one of the pressure chambers overlying one of the actuators. Rigid walls 518 that extend vertically from the wafer 404 form walls of one or more pressure chambers. These walls help hold fluid received from the inlet 128 in the pressure chambers overlying the actuators and the flexible membranes that respond to the actuators. The flexible membranes 530A-530E may be formed from a polysilicon material, or alternatively from SU-8 polymer or other silicon layers.

[0027] The term “alignment” as used in this document to describe the relationship of an aperture to a pressure chamber in a bonded composite wafer refers to the position of each aperture in an aperture array with reference to a longitudinal axis, shown by axis 540, placed between walls 518 of a corresponding actuator area in an actuator array. Longitudinal axis 540 bisects each actuator area 524 between walls 518, although actuator embodiments with different geometries may have different alignment axes. The actual position of the center of an aperture after the bonding process is completed may differ from the aligned positions along axis 540. An alignment error describes the difference in position from the center of the actual position of the aperture from the aligned positions on longitudinal axis 540, indicated by arrows 544. An aperture with a sufficiently large alignment error prevents ink in a pressure chamber from being ejected through an aperture during operation of a printhead. Alignment errors may also refer to the difference in position between the center of an aperture with respect to the ends 542A and 542B of the longitudinal axis 540.

[0028] FIG. 6 depicts a single actuator, pressure chamber, and aperture assembly 610 taken along a cross-sectional view from FIG. 5. Actuator assembly 610 includes silicon substrate in wafer 104, actuator 646, pressure chamber 534, and intermediate layers, such as flexible membrane 530A and rigid walls 518. Bonded polymer aperture layer 116 overlies pressure chamber 534 and includes antiwetting coating 206. An optional adhesive 612 aids in bonding the aperture layer 116 to the exposed top surfaces of rigid walls 518. One or more insulating layers 640 may also be deposited on the wafer substrate 104. The insulating layer 640 may comprise silicon dioxide and silicon nitride. A conductive layer, comprising polysilicon in FIG. 6, forms a bottom electrode 644 in actuator 646. The diaphragm 530A and electrode 644 form an actuator 646 that may eject ink through aperture 136. The actuator 646 also includes a cavity 652 formed between membrane 530A and electrode 644. Cavity 652 provides space for diaphragm 530A to deflect towards and away from electrode 644. Although the example embodiment of FIG. 6 employs an electrostatic actuator, devices incorporating a piezoelectric actuator, thermal actuator, or any other actuator suitable for ejecting ink drops may be used.

[0029] The structure of a bonded and separated die site operates in a printhead in the following manner. The inlet 128 (FIG. 5) receives fluid from a fluid reservoir (not shown) and enables the fluid to flow from inlet 128 through channel 532 to the pressure chamber 534 over the actuator 646. An electrical signal activates an actuator electrode 644 to cause the diaphragm 530A to move towards the actuator electrode, although other types of excitation may be used to actuate other types of actuators. This deflection expands the volume of fluidic chamber 534 and decreases the pressure in the chamber 534 so fluid flows through ink inlet 128 into the pressure chamber 534. In response to the activation signal returning to an inactive state, the actuator membrane 530A returns to an equilibrium position. This action urges a portion of the fluid in the pressure chamber 534 through aperture 136. In inkjet embodiments, the fluid may be liquid ink that is ejected from aperture 136 in the form of a drop. A completed printhead may incorporate one or more of the bonded dies produced by process 300.

METHOD FOR FORMING ANAPERTURE AND ACTUATORLAYER FOR AN INKJET PRINTHEAD TECHNICAL FIELD This disclosure relates generally to methods for manufac turing components used in inkjet printheads, and more par ticularly, to methods for fabricating composite layers used in inkjet printheads. BACKGROUND Micro-electromechanical systems (MEMS) are mechani cal systems that are micromachined in silicon and may be optionally integrated with control electronic circuits. MEMS are generally categorized as either microsensor or microac tuator systems, depending on the application. MEMS incor porate electrostatic, electromagnetic, thermoelastic, piezo electric, or piezoresistive effects in the operations of the systems. One use for MEMS devices is in drop on demand inkjet technology that has been employed in commercial products, Such as printers, plotters, and facsimile machines. Generally, an inkjet image is formed by the selective activation of inkjets within a printhead to eject ink onto an ink receiving member. To facilitate manufacture of an inkjet array printhead, an array of inkjet ejectors can be formed from multiple laminated plates or sheets. These sheets are configured with arrays of ink droplet ejectors. Each ejector may include structures Such as an actuator, pressure chamber, outlet, and aperture nozzle. These structures are formed from the superposition of the multiple laminated structural layers. An example of a lami nated layer inkjet array for a printhead includes a silicon layer bonded to an aperture layer formed on a polymer material, Such as polyimide orthermoplastic. The silicon layer includes an array of actuators. Each actuator has an associated ink inlet, diaphragm, and pressure chamber area. The polymer aperture layer includes an aperture in the form of a nozzle. Walls are formed on the silicon layer to for a pressure cham ber for each operator and the polymeraperture layer is bonded to the walls to enclose the pressure chamber and establish fluid communication between each aperture in the aperture layer and each pressure chamber formed on the silicon layer. Once formed, each actuator in the array of actuators may be selectively activated to deform the diaphragm and expel an ink droplet from the pressure chamber through the aperture. The process for bonding the polymer aperture plate to the walls extending from the silicon layer requires alignment of the apertures in the aperture layer with the silicon layer. Existing manufacturing processes produce actuator arrays by forming a plurality of actuator arrays on a silicon wafer and then cutting the silicon wafer to separate the actuator arrays from one another. The inlets, diaphragms, and walls are then formed on the actuator arrays and the polymer aperture plate is bonded to the walls extending from the silicon plate. Known methods of aligning apertures in an aperture plate to actuators and their associated structure on the silicon layer often result in alignment errors of at least five microns in magnitude. Increased efficiencies and improved precision in alignment in the manufacture of the MEMS printheads would be beneficial to the fields of imaging in general, and inkjet printing in particular. SUMMARY An improved method for manufacturing components use ful for inkjet printheads has been developed. The method

As used herein, the term “wafer refers to a planar material sheet adapted to have multiple repeated instances of a structural pattern formed on and through the surface of the wafer. A common example of a wafer is a silicon wafer used in the fabrication of microelectronics and micro electro-mechanical system (MEMS) devices. Common examples of these wafers have approximately circular shapes with diameters between 25 mm and 450 mm and thicknesses of approximately 275um to 950 um. While the wafer is often primarily composed of a silicon Substrate, wafers may also include planar layers of other materials, such as metals. Selected regions of a wafer may include chemicals diffused into the wafer substrate in a process known as doping. While wafers with silicon sub strates are widely used in industry, other materials, including metallic crystals formed from elements of the III-V group in the periodic table, may also be used to form wafers. A pho toresist material, which is typically a polymeric material, may optionally cover a wafer Substrate. A positive photoresist material becomes soluble to chemical solvents in response to exposure to radiation. A negative photoresist material becomes insoluble to chemical solvents once exposed to radiation, typically actinic radiation. One example of a nega tive photoresist commonly used in microfluidic applications is SU-8, a polymer that may coat a wafer in thicknesses ranging between about 0.1 micrometers and 2 millimeters. As used herein, a “microfluidic structure' may refer to a variety of channels, passageways, openings, or chambers formed in one or more layers of material adapted to transport and hold a quantity of fluid such as ink. Typical microfluidic structures have dimensions ranging from about 500 microns to less than 1 micronin size. Photolithographic techniques may be used to pattern and etch structures, such as microfluidic channels and chambers, into photoresist materials as well as the underlying wafer. Various deposition techniques including vapor depo sition, sputtering, spin coating, plating, and other techniques known to the art may also form structures, including microf luidic channels and chambers, on the Surface of the underly ing wafer. As used herein, the term “die site' refers to a defined section disposed within a larger layer of material. The layer is typically a wafer, and each die site contains one or more structures that remain intact after a die site is cut from the layer. A plurality of die sites are formed on a wafer, and each die site includes one instance of a structural pattern formed on the wafer. A wafer is typically formed with a plurality of die sites arranged in a pattern, such as a two dimensional grid. An inter-die region separates the die sites to enable cutting of each die site from the layer without damag ing the structures in the die site. Die sites often have rectan gular shapes with the same structure repeated in each die site on a layer in many common embodiments. A wafer 104 having multiple die sites that are arranged in a grid pattern is shown in FIG. 1A. Two die sites 108A and 108B are shown in the magnified view of FIG. 1B. Each die site includes ten actuators 112 having open pressure cham bers formed over them. The actuators and pressure chambers are arranged in an array having two rows with each row having five actuators and pressure chambers. An ink inlet 128 that is etched through the wafer 104 in each die site enables an external fluid source to be coupled to the pressure chambers. Inter-die region 110 separates die site 108A from die site 108B. The remaining die sites are similarly separated. Thus, cutting through the inter-die regions 110 of the wafer 104 separates the die sites from one another. Each separated piece of the wafer that contains an actuator array is called a die, and

A polymer layer 116 that has been prepared for bonding to the wafer 104 to cover the microfluidic structures constructed on the layer is shown in FIG.1C. The polymer film is typically a plate or a sheet of a polymer, such as a polyimide or ther moplastic, cut to approximately the same shape and size as the wafer 104. The polymer film may include a single layer, or multiple layers that incorporate adhesive layers for bonding with the wafer, and an optional anti-wetting coating on an outward facing surface of the polymer film. Polymer film layer 116 has a size and shape corresponding to wafer 104. A plurality of aperture arrays are arranged in a grid pattern that corresponds to the die site grid pattern in wafer 104. FIG. 1D shows a magnified view of two aperture arrays 124A and 124B in polymer film 116. Each aperture array includes ten apertures 136 that are arranged in two rows with each row having five apertures. Region 132 separates the aperture array 108A from aperture array 108B. The remaining aperture arrays are similarly separated. Each aperture array is posi tioned at a location that corresponds to an actuator array die site in wafer 104. The apertures are formed in the polymer layer 116 using various techniques, which include laserablation. An example of a laser ablation technique includes ablating an aperture in the layer 116 with an excimer laser. A cross-sectional view of the layer 116 is shown in FIG. 2. The surface 212 of layer 116 is configured to bond to the structures on the wafer that form the pressure chambers. Surface 216 of the layer 116 has been covered with an antiwetting coating 206 that is deposited on polymer layer 116 prior to ablation of the layer to form the apertures. The antiwetting coating 206 resists adhesion of ink to the exposed surface of the aperture layer during printing operations. FIG.3 depicts a process 300 that forms multiple dies for the manufacture of inkjet printheads. Process 300 begins with the construction of microfluidic structure on a silicon wafer

US 8,684,499 B2 5 (block 304) and the formation of the apertures in the aperture arrays on the polymer layer (block 308). The die sites one the wafer are then aligned with the aperture arrays on the polymer film (block 312). The alignment may be facilitated with align ment features that were formed in the circumference of the wafer and the polymer layer during the processes performed in blocks 304 and 308. The alignment process places each aperture in the polymer film layer in fluid communication with a corresponding pressure chamber on the wafer. Follow ing the alignment, the polymer layer is bonded to the wafer (block 316). After the bonding process is completed, the bonded wafer and polymer layer may be cut, or diced, into individual actuator array and aperture plate dies (block 320). The bonding of the wafer and the polymer layer may be achieved with a thin layer of epoxy interposed between the polymer layer and bonding Surfaces on the wafer. A Suitable epoxy for the bonding process includes Epon Repoxy, as well as alternative adhesives including phenolic, polyimide, and acrylic adhesive layers. The example bonding process includes the application of heat and pressure to the wafer and polymer film layers. The heat and pressure may cause an uneventhermal expansion between the wafer and the polymer layer. This uneven expansion may place stress on the wafer and cause the wafer to crack. To address this uneven expan sion and reduce the risk of wafer cracking, gaps, such as the gap 120 shown in FIG. 1D, may be included in the layer 116 to separate the aperture arrays in the polymer layer. The gaps provide an area between each aperture array where the poly mer layer may expand while reducing stress applied to the wafer. After the wafer and the polymer film have been bonded together, they form a multi-layered composite wafer such as the composite wafer 404 shown in FIG. 4A. In that figure, the polymer film 116 has been aligned and bonded to the under lying silicon wafer 104. Each aperture array in the polymer film 116 is adequately aligned with a corresponding pressure chamber in a die site in the wafer 104 to enable each aperture in the polymer layer to be in fluid communication with a pressure chamber overlying an actuator in an actuator array at each die site on the wafer 404. This bonded composite wafer may then be cut along the inter-die regions of the wafer 104 to form the bonded dies 432 shown in FIG. 4B. Typical dicing methods include cutting along the inter-die regions with a mechanical saw or a laser cutter. Thus, the process of FIG. 3 is an efficient method for manufacturing dies for inkjet print heads. The process 300 may produce bonded dies 432 having alignment errors between each aperture and pressure cham ber of less than one micron in magnitude. A portion of the bonded composite wafer 404 is shown in FIG. 5. Each aperture 136 (shown in phantom in the figure) is aligned with a pressure chamber, such as 530A, that overlies an actuator 524 in an actuator array. These walls help hold fluid received from the inlet 128 in the pressure chambers overlying the actuators and the flexible membranes that respond to the actuators. scoring_policy.subjective_metrics: The Judge returns 0, 0.5, or 1 for each scored criterion using its own levels. G3-G5 additionally follow the synchronized zero-score rule below. The Judge does not calculate weights or totals.
scoring_policy.input_mode: Case source materials, task requirements, and the candidate response; no expert annotations or case-specific scoring layer.
scoring_policy.validation_checks: Case identity, input completeness, consultation of legal provisions, and verification of quotations are evaluation checks, not separately weighted criteria.

steps: Distribute the common-layer budget among applicable groups in the ratio foundation:amendment:argument = 25:20:55. If an entire group is not applicable, renormalize the remaining original group budgets.

Within the argument group, distribute its budget among applicable issue types according to argument_types.relative_weight. Inventive step is one complete issue type; its budget does not vary with the number of applicable inventive-step subcriteria.

Within each group other than argument, or within each argument issue type, distribute the budget among applicable criteria in proportion to each criterion's relative_weight. Use unrounded weights throughout the calculation.
weight_allocation.final_score: round(100 * C, 1), only when every applicable criterion is scored
weight_allocation.baseline_warning: The all-applicable percentages are illustrative only. Do not drop inapplicable entries from those percentages and renormalize the resulting flat list.
weight_allocation.calibration_note: These weights are initial design values, not proportions prescribed by the Word standard, and have not yet been calibrated against the new 100-case set.

applicability.amendment_rule: G3-G5 activate together when the candidate actually amends the claims and are scored using the Word levels. If the synchronized zero-score rule applies, all three remain active with score 0. Otherwise, when no amendment is made, all three are not_applicable.
applicability.argument_rule: Determine applicability of each G6 criterion from the complete OA, the actual points of dispute, the jurisdiction, and the necessary reasoning steps. A single inventive-step objection may require several subcriteria. A missing candidate response does not make an existing issue not applicable.
applicability.not_applicable: Use status=not_applicable and score=null only when a conditional criterion does not apply; provide the reason and references to source materials. Only not_applicable releases allocated weight.

amendment_zero_rule.trigger: The Judge determines that the claims should be amended, but the candidate OAR has not chosen an amendment strategy.
amendment_zero_rule.evidence_requirement: Each of G3-G5 must cite the case basis showing why amendment is needed and evidence that the candidate did not choose that strategy. A difference between pre_claim and post_claim alone is insufficient to infer that amendment is required.
amendment_zero_rule.defect_description_requirement: Each criterion's defect description must identify its current metric ID and explain that the zero score is required by this synchronized rule.
amendment_zero_rule.scope: Do not mark these three criteria not_applicable or redistribute the amendment budget. G2, G6, and all other scoring rules continue to apply as specified.

result_contract.scored: A score of 0, 0.5, or 1 and verifiable evidence references are required.
result_contract.unscored: not_applicable, not_evaluable, and failed require score=null. Conditional not_applicable results require a reason and source references.
result_contract.failure_handling: not_evaluable and failed retain their allocated shares and block the final score. Do not redistribute their shares to scored criteria or remove an inventive-step type because one subcriterion cannot be evaluated.
result_contract.consistency_checks: Validate required criteria, consistent applicability of G3-G5, compliance with the synchronized zero-score rule, and evidence fields. Programmatic checks do not replace semantic review.

audit_fields.common_group_allocation: Group budgets, active criteria, and argument.types with issue-type budgets and subcriteria.
audit_fields.common_allocated_weights: Allocated weights including shares reserved for not_evaluable or failed criteria.
audit_fields.common_effective_weights: Weights actually contributing to the score; not_applicable, not_evaluable, and failed have effective weight 0. Failed or unevaluable applicable criteria still block a final total.

scoring_policy.duplicate_defect_rule: Assign each minimal defect to one primary criterion rather than penalizing it repeatedly across criteria. The explicitly required synchronized G3-G5 zero scores are a policy exception; each must identify the current criterion and the reason for the rule-based zero score.

metrics.name: Accuracy of understanding the case facts and Office Action
metrics.evaluation_object: Whether the application, its current claims, the Office Action, and the relevant cited documents are correctly understood, and whether the validity of the grounds for objection is correctly assessed.

levels.1: Correctly understands the application, the claims, the technical features, and their relationships; accurately understands the meaning of the grounds for objection and accurately assesses whether they are valid.
levels.0.5: Correctly assesses the main technical solution, the grounds for objection, and the points open to argument, but has localized misunderstandings of noncritical facts, feature relationships, or document content; these do not change the main direction of the response and can be corrected locally.
levels.0: Misunderstands the technical solution of the application, feature relationships, or the Office Action; makes errors such as confusing the original claims, the current claims, and the proposed amended claims.

metrics.activation_condition: Required for every case.

metrics.name: Reasonableness of the overall response strategy
metrics.evaluation_object: Whether the choice between relying solely on argument and proactively amending the claims is reasonable; if proactive amendment is chosen, whether the choice of claims to amend is reasonable and whether any improper admissions are made.

levels.1: The choice of argument alone, amendment, or a combination of the two is supported by the case; the claims selected for treatment are appropriate, and the overall strategy addresses the core issues in the Office Action; no unsupported, materially adverse admissions are made.
levels.0.5: The main response approach is reasonable, but there are localized inappropriate choices in the treatment of noncore claims that do not affect the main position.
levels.0: The main response approach cannot address the core issues, for example, persisting with argument alone when the arguments lack a valid basis, or failing to include core claims requiring amendment in the strategy; makes adverse admissions that lack a basis in the Office Action and materially weaken the position on the main scope of protection.

metrics.activation_condition: Required for every case.

metrics.name: Effectiveness of claim amendments in addressing the issues identified in the Office Action [if amended]
metrics.evaluation_object: Whether the claim amendments themselves resolve the issues targeted by the Office Action, assessed separately from the quality of the response statement.

levels.1: The specific amendments correspond to the issues identified in the Office Action, and the amended claims, together with the response statement, are sufficient to overcome those defects.
levels.0.5: The amendments resolve the core defects identified in the Office Action, but the treatment of noncore defects is incomplete and requires localized correction.
levels.0: The core defects identified in the Office Action remain after amendment; or the amendments have no substantive connection to the defects identified in the Office Action.

metrics.activation_condition: G3-G5 activate together when the candidate actually amends the claims and are scored using the Word levels. If the synchronized zero-score rule applies, all three remain active with score 0. Otherwise, when no amendment is made, all three are not_applicable.

metrics.name: Proportionality of claim amendments and preservation of the scope of protection [if amended]
metrics.evaluation_object: Whether there is avoidable loss of protection while reasonably addressing the Office Action, assessed against the original protection objectives of the case.

levels.1: Added limitations, claim deletions, and other scope adjustments are reasonably necessary or reflect supported strategic tradeoffs; there is no unnecessary narrowing that can be clearly demonstrated from the case materials.
levels.0.5: There are individual unnecessary additional limitations or losses of noncore claims, but the main protection objectives of the original application are not materially affected; a less restrictive and equally reasonable localized adjustment can be specifically identified.
levels.0: Despite the existence of a supported, reasonable approach involving less narrowing, introduces significantly unnecessary limitations, deletes important claims, or abandons key protected subject matter, materially harming the main protection objectives.

metrics.activation_condition: G3-G5 activate together when the candidate actually amends the claims and are scored using the Word levels. If the synchronized zero-score rule applies, all three remain active with score 0. Otherwise, when no amendment is made, all three are not_applicable.

metrics.name: Legality and formal compliance of claim amendments [if amended]
metrics.evaluation_object: Whether amendments have a basis in the original disclosure and comply with amendment rules; whether clarity, support, antecedent basis, and claim dependencies meet the applicable requirements.

levels.1: The amended claim content and combinations have a verifiable basis in the original disclosure and comply with the applicable amendment rules; the amended claims are clear and supported by the description, with correct terminology, antecedent basis, and claim dependencies.
levels.0.5: The amendments have a basis in the original disclosure and the scope of protection can be determined, but there are correctable localized wording or citation-form defects; correction does not change the substantive technical solution.
levels.0: The amendments exceed the permissible scope, introduce content or combinations lacking a basis in the original disclosure, or create generalizations unsupported by the description; substantive errors in key wording, feature relationships, or claim dependencies make the scope of protection indeterminate or the technical solution untenable.

metrics.activation_condition: G3-G5 activate together when the candidate actually amends the claims and are scored using the Word levels. If the synchronized zero-score rule applies, all three remain active with score 0. Otherwise, when no amendment is made, all three are not_applicable.

metrics.name: Quality of analysis of the closest prior art and distinguishing technical features

levels.1: Accepts or challenges the examiner's identification of the closest prior art on a supported basis; correctly identifies the specific differences between the claims and the closest prior art, correctly analyzes and defines the distinguishing technical features, and clearly and sufficiently performs the feature comparison needed to support that conclusion.
levels.0.5: Correctly identifies the closest prior art and the main distinguishing technical features, but some comparisons, feature relationships, or explanations of the supporting basis are incomplete; these can be supplemented using the existing materials.
levels.0: The identification of distinguishing technical features is untenable, or distinguishing technical features decisive to the conclusion are omitted; rejects the starting point for comparison without a basis; merely asserts that "differences exist" without substantively comparing the features at the core of the dispute.

metrics.name: Quality of analysis of the technical effects of the distinguishing technical features and the technical problem actually solved

levels.1: Uses the description, appropriate evidence, or reasonable technical analysis to explain how the distinguishing features and their interaction produce the relevant technical effects; accurately defines the technical problem actually solved on that basis; accurately assesses whether the examiner has incorporated the means of solving the problem disclosed in the application into the definition of the technical problem, and reasonably addresses disagreements with the examiner's definition of that problem.
levels.0.5: The main assessment of the technical effects of the distinguishing technical features and the technical problem actually solved is supported, but the explanation of the causal relationship between features and effects, or of the relationship between the effects achieved by the distinguishing technical features in the invention and the technical problem actually solved, is insufficient; the main argument can be completed by elaborating on the existing basis.
levels.0: Incorrectly defines the technical effects that the distinguishing technical features can achieve in the invention or the technical problem actually solved, or misunderstands or reasons incorrectly about the derivation connecting the two, resulting in an incorrect key foundation for the inventive step response.

metrics.name: Quality of analysis and rebuttal concerning other cited documents and common general knowledge

levels.1: For cited documents or common general knowledge used to supply the distinguishing technical features, accurately analyzes their disclosed content, the functions of their features, and the differences from the distinguishing technical features of the application; acceptance or challenge of a finding of common general knowledge is consistent with the evidence and applicable rules on the burden of proof.
levels.0.5: Correctly assesses the functions of features in other cited documents and the direction of the rebuttal, but inadequately analyzes localized correspondences or the basis for the finding of common general knowledge.
levels.0: The substantive analysis of content used to supply key distinguishing technical features is incorrect, or the main differences relied on for rebuttal are untenable; merely asserts that something is "not disclosed" or "not common general knowledge," without the explanation or evidence needed to support the core conclusion.

metrics.name: Quality of analysis and rebuttal concerning technical teachings and reasons for combination

levels.1: Addresses the examiner's actual reasons for combination and, in light of the technical effects of the distinguishing technical features and the actual technical problem, sufficiently analyzes the motivation to modify, technical teachings, conditions for combination, or barriers to combination, reaching a correctly supported conclusion on whether the overall claimed solution is obvious; explicitly checks whether the cited documents are compatible in their technical environments, operating principles, functions, and cooperative relationships; accurately identifies whether the examiner has used the application as a roadmap to reconstruct a combination of prior art.
levels.0.5: Provides effective analysis directly relevant to the reasons for combination, but inadequately explains some combination steps, functional relationships, or barriers to combination; the main direction of the argument is valid.
levels.0: Fails to effectively address the reasons for combination that determine the examination conclusion; asserts that combination is impossible solely because of differences in technical fields, technical problems, or effects; or fails to clearly explain why a person skilled in the art could not arrive at the overall claimed solution by following the stated reasons.

metrics.name: Quality of the substantive response to novelty objections
metrics.notes: The "four samenesses" are not a mandatory structure requiring rebuttal of each element.

levels.1: Addresses the novelty objection by analyzing the claims and relevant cited documents under the applicable principle of comparison with each reference separately, identifying differences that affect the novelty determination and their supporting basis; where amendments are used, explains why the amended solution is not fully disclosed by the cited content.
levels.0.5: Identifies supported substantive technical differences, but inadequately explains feature correspondences, disclosed content, or the significance of the differences; the argument can be completed by elaborating on the existing materials.
levels.0: Fails to develop a substantive argument capable of supporting novelty; the main reasons concern only superficial differences in use, technical field, problem, or effect and cannot explain substantive differences in the technical solution; or relies on untenable feature differences to support the conclusion.

metrics.name: Quality of the substantive response to subject-matter eligibility objections

levels.1: Provides a supported analysis of the specific grounds for subject-matter exclusion in relation to the solution defined by the claims, sufficiently explaining why the original or amended solution satisfies the corresponding subject-matter requirements.
levels.0.5: The direction of the subject-matter assessment is correct and the specific solution is discussed, but some elements or relationships decisive to that assessment are insufficiently explained.
levels.0: Fails to substantively address the specific grounds for exclusion; substitutes labels such as "involves technology" or "uses a computer" for the necessary analysis; or the stated reasons cannot support a conclusion that the solution satisfies the applicable subject-matter requirements.

metrics.name: Quality of the substantive response to sufficiency of disclosure, enablement, or written description objections

levels.1: Accurately distinguishes the disclosure or description defects actually identified in the OA and, using the original application documents and knowledge or evidence that may lawfully be relied on, sufficiently explains that the corresponding requirements are satisfied or how a lawful adjustment addresses the defect.
levels.0.5: Identifies original content or evidence directly relevant to the defect and takes the correct direction in the response, but inadequately explains the implementation path, the correspondence to the description, or the extent of support.
levels.0: Fails to explain the core implementation or description obstacle identified; merely asserts that the subject matter "has already been disclosed"; substitutes new content incapable of remedying the original defect for the required disclosure, or relies on reasons unrelated to the actual defect to support the conclusion.

metrics.name: Quality of the substantive response to clarity, support, and claim-form objections

levels.1: Accurately locates the identified problem with feature descriptions, protection boundaries, support for generalization, or claim form, and sufficiently addresses the corresponding defect through supported explanations or explanations of amendments.
levels.0.5: Provides an explanation or explanation of amendments that addresses the specific problem in the correct direction, but the correspondence or reasons for compliance are incomplete.
levels.0: Fails to substantively explain the specific defect; merely asserts in general terms that the claims are "clear," "supported," or "compliant"; or the argument fails to explain why the core ambiguity, support gap, or formal error has been addressed.

metrics.name: Quality of the substantive response to objections that an independent claim lacks essential technical features

levels.1: Accurately explains the technical problem being solved, the essential features, and their functional relationships, and uses the original disclosure to sufficiently demonstrate that the existing independent claim defines a complete solution or to explain how adding the relevant features completes that solution.
levels.0.5: The main assessment of the technical problem and essential features is correct, but the explanation of why the existing features are sufficient, why the added features are necessary, or how the features function together is insufficient.
levels.0: Fails to substantively analyze necessity; incorrectly treats optional features as essential or essential features as optional and bases the main conclusion on that error; the core argument cannot explain how the independent claim defines a complete solution to the stated technical problem.

metrics.name: Logical coherence of the overall argument
metrics.evaluation_object: Connections and consistency across paragraphs, claims, and different grounds of argument; the quality of reasoning on an individual point of dispute falls primarily under item 6.

levels.1: The main arguments, evidence, and conclusions throughout the text are clearly connected, the logical chain is complete, and the different grounds of argument are mutually coherent; the response statement is consistent with the final claims.
levels.0.5: The main positions and conclusions are consistent, but there are noncritical gaps in logical connections, repetitions, or localized inconsistencies in wording; the intended meaning can be clearly determined from context.
levels.0: Core arguments or factual premises conflict and cannot hold simultaneously, or the logical chain is incomplete or contains gaps; the main conclusion contradicts the evidence presented; key limitations relied on in the response statement are absent from the final claims being pursued, causing a mismatch in the subject of the main argument.

metrics.activation_condition: Required for every case.

metrics.name: Completeness of the response to the Office Action
metrics.evaluation_object: Whether all issues mentioned in the response statement have been addressed, without reassessing the sufficiency of responses already made.

levels.1: All Office Action objections, affected claims, and independent points of dispute requiring treatment are explicitly addressed; the scope of consolidated responses, amendments, deletions, or reliance on common reasons is clear, with no omissions.
levels.0.5: All core issues are addressed, but noncore objections or secondary issues affecting noncore claims are omitted.
levels.0: The response omits a major type of Office Action objection, so that the response as a whole fails to cover the main issues that must be resolved in this round; merely naming an issue without providing any treatment does not count as addressing it.

metrics.activation_condition: Required for every case.

metrics.name: Completeness of deliverables and conformity with textual conventions
metrics.notes: This item combines four checks: required documents; numbering and versions; terminology and written expression; formatting and grammar. Terminology errors here concern expression and word choice; actual misunderstandings of technical concepts fall under item 1, and substantive conflicts in position fall under item 7.

levels.1: All documents required by the task are provided, including the required amended text and comparison materials where amendments are actually made; requests, claims, cited documents, figures, application numbers, and versions are correctly numbered and matched; terminology is standard and consistent, expression is professional, clear, and concise, grammar, wording, hierarchy, and punctuation follow conventions, and no unresolved placeholders remain.
levels.0.5: All required documents are provided, and the final text for submission and the objects cited can be uniquely identified, but there are localized numbering typos, inconsistent terminology, mildly colloquial language, redundancy, typographical errors, ungrammatical sentences, or formatting problems; these do not change the technical meaning, requests, or reference targets and can be corrected locally.
levels.0: A required document is missing; the final claim version, request, or key reference target cannot be determined; unfilled placeholders remain in key locations; or problems with language, terminology, numbering, or layout prevent accurate understanding of the main content or require substantial rewriting.

metrics.activation_condition: Required for every case.

metrics.name: Compliance with the applicable jurisdiction and examination rules
metrics.evaluation_object: Whether the legal assessment standards, response logic, amendment principles, and procedural rules used in the response apply under the laws and regulations of the country corresponding to the case.

levels.1: The assessment standards, response logic, amendment principles, and procedural treatment actually used are consistent with the jurisdiction, procedural stage, and applicable version of the law for the case; where legal authorities are cited, their content and scope of application are correct.
levels.0.5: The substantive assessment standards and procedural treatment are correct, but there are isolated errors in statutory provision numbers, names of laws, version labels, or legal terminology; correcting them does not change the assessment standards, response conclusions, or procedural validity.
levels.0: Applies substantive rules from an inapplicable jurisdiction, procedural stage, or version of the law; misunderstands key legal requirements, examination rules, or procedural restrictions, making the main grounds of response, amendment principles, or procedural treatment untenable.

metrics.activation_condition: Required for every case.

metrics.name: Authenticity of factual statements and citations [hallucination control]
metrics.evaluation_object: Whether the response asserts the existence of content, facts, data, Office Action objections, or sources that do not actually exist. Supported technical inferences, explicitly labeled assumptions, and proactive analysis of genuine issues not mentioned in the OA are not hallucinations. Misinterpretation of real content falls primarily under item 1.

levels.1: Factual statements and citations can be verified from the corresponding materials or real sources; citations support the stated views, and reasonable inferences are distinguished from the original disclosure and established facts; no Office Action objections, technical content, data, or sources are fabricated, and no nonexistent Office Action objections are answered.
levels.0.5: No facts or sources are fabricated, but the scope of support from individual real sources is overstated; narrowing the statement corrects the problem, and the relevant conclusion remains sufficiently supported by the real grounds already identified.
levels.0: Fabricates application content, cited-document content, experimental data, facts, Office Action objections, or citation sources, or answers nonexistent Office Action objections.

metrics.activation_condition: Required for every case.

# Description

CROSS-REFERENCE TO RELATED APPLICATIONS

[0001] This application is a divisional of U.S. patent application Ser. No. 13/039,559 filed on Mar. 3, 2011. The entire disclosure of the above application is incorporated herein by reference.
FIELD

[0002] The present disclosure generally relates to a system for treating exhaust gases. More particularly, a system for interconnecting and supporting various exhaust treatment devices is described.

[0003] BACKGROUND

[0004] To reduce the quantity of NOx and particulate matter emitted to the atmosphere during internal combustion engine operation, a number of exhaust aftertreatment devices have been developed. A need for exhaust aftertreatment systems particularly arises when diesel combustion processes are implemented. Typical aftertreatment systems for diesel engine exhaust may include one or more of a diesel particulate filter (DPF), a selective catalytic reduction (SCR) system, a hydrocarbon (HC) injector, and a diesel oxidation catalyst (DOC).

[0005] During engine operation, the DPF traps soot emitted by the engine and reduces the emission of particulate matter (PM). Over time, the DPF becomes loaded and begins to clog. Periodically, regeneration or oxidation of the trapped soot in the DPF is required for proper operation. To regenerate the DPF, relatively high exhaust temperatures in combination with an ample amount of oxygen in the exhaust stream are needed to oxidize the soot trapped in the filter.

[0006] The DOC is typically used to generate heat useful for regenerating the soot loaded DPF. When hydrocarbons (HC) are sprayed over the DOC at or above a specific light-off temperature, the HC will oxidize. This reaction is highly exothermic and the exhaust gases are heated during light-off. The heated exhaust gases are used to regenerate the DPF.

[0007] Over time, however, the DPF may degrade and become less effective. Replacement of the DPF or another exhaust treatment device may be necessary. Alternatively, the exhaust treatment device may be serviced or otherwise rejuvenated when the exhaust treatment device is removed from the system.

[0008] DPFs, DOCs and the like have been coupled to relatively small displacement internal combustion engines for automotive use. It may also be desirable to treat the exhaust emitted from engines in other applications including diesel locomotives, stationary power plants and marine vessels. These systems may be equipped with relatively large diesel compression engines. The exhaust mass flow rate from the larger engines may be more than ten times the maximum flow rate typically provided. The size and weight of the exhaust treatment devices required for large engines may make the components unwieldy and very costly. Therefore, a need may exist in the art for an arrangement to easily service and support the devices for treating the exhaust output from a large diesel engine. Some of the exhaust treatment devices such as DPFs are relatively fragile and susceptible to fracture. Care should be taken during DPF replacement and operation to avoid impact loading. Furthermore, it may be desirable to maintain a predetermined exhaust flow direction through the exhaust treatment device and also a predetermined rotational alignment between exhaust treatment devices.
SUMMARY

[0009] This section provides a general summary of the disclosure, and is not a comprehensive disclosure of its full scope or all of its features.

[0010] An exhaust treatment system includes an emissions treatment device having an upstream end and a downstream end for treating exhaust emitted from an internal combustion engine. The exhaust treatment system includes a frame adapted to support first and second portions of the exhaust treatment system. The first and second portions of the system are spaced apart from one another. The emissions treatment device interconnects the first and second portions and is in receipt of exhaust from the first portion and provides treated exhaust to the second portion. A first bracket is fixed to the frame and includes one of a protrusion and a receptacle. A second bracket is adapted to be fixed to the emissions treatment device and includes the other of the protrusion and the receptacle. The protrusion is positioned within the receptacle when the emissions treatment device is properly positioned. The protrusion interferes with one of the second bracket and the emissions treatment device to preclude assembly when the emissions treatment device is improperly positioned.

[0011] An exhaust treatment system includes first, second and third emissions treatment devices positioned in series fluid communication with one another. The second emissions treatment device is removable from between the first and third emissions treatment devices. A first bracket is coupled to one of the first and third emissions treatment devices and includes one of a protrusion and a receptacle. A second bracket is fixed to the second emissions treatment device and includes the other of the protrusion and the receptacle. The protrusion is positioned within the receptacle when the second emissions treatment device is properly positioned. The protrusion interferes with one of the first bracket and the second emissions treatment device to preclude assembly when the second emissions treatment device is improperly positioned.

DRAWINGS

[0013] The drawings described herein are for illustrative purposes only of selected embodiments and not all possible implementations, and are not intended to limit the scope of the present disclosure.

[0014] FIG. 1 is a schematic depicting an exhaust aftertreatment system including a poka-yoke mounting arrangement;
