EXAMPLES
The examples below describe specific temperatures, incubation times and buffers.
However, the conditions are not intended to be limiting. A person of ordinary skill in the art
would know that the human gDNA exemplified here as a starting material for enriching various
sequences therefrom is not intended to be limiting nor should the extent to which pH, buffer and
salt conditions and incubation times could be varied to effect a similar degree of hybridization or
amplification be limited to the conditions specified below. Similarly, the description of biotin as
an affinity domain is not intended to be limiting. Specific adaptors with specific cleavable sites
are also described below by way of an example and is not intended to be limiting. An order of
steps is described as an example. It will be understood that order of steps may be modified.
Moreover, certain steps may be added or deleted as expedient.
Example 1: A method for enriching for target sequence for sequencing with one
15 target isolation probes.
Human gDNA (1ug) was sheared with a Covaris device following the manufacturer's
protocol for 300bp fragments (Figure 1 (1)). The sheared DNA was added to 25ul hybridization
reaction buffer containing 20nmol of target isolation probe which was 100 bases in length and
associated with biotin where the 100 base sequence was complementary to the 100nt target
sequence (Figure 1 (2)). The hybridization reaction was performed according to John, et al.
BioTechniques, 44, 259-264 (2008). After hybridization, the target isolation probe/target DNA
duplexes were bound to 50ul of hydrophilic streptavidin beads (New England Biolabs, Ipswich,
MA) for 30 minutes (Figure 1 (3)) and washed with standard BW Buffer (5mM Tris-HCI (pH 7.5),
0.5mM EDTA, 1M NaCl).
As utilized throughout, a "reaction mixture" means a solution containing all the
necessary reactants for performing a reaction, which may include, but not be limited to,
buffering agents to maintain pH at a selected level during a reaction, enzymes, substrates,
salts, co-factors, scavengers, and the like.

The beads were resuspended in a 50ul reaction mix containing 1X NEBuffer 4, 2.5 U
Exonuclease T (New England Biolabs, Ipswich, MA) and 2.5 U Exonuclease 1 (New England
Biolabs, Ipswich, MA) and incubated for 10 minutes at 37°C. The magnetic beads were
washed and resuspended in 50ul of 1X NEBuffer 2 containing 30 units of RecJf (New England
Biolabs, Ipswich, MA) and incubated for 10 minutes at 20°C (Figure 1 (4)).
The magnetic beads were washed and resuspended in 50ul of dA-Tailing reaction mix
(New England Biolabs, Ipswich, MA) and incubated for 30 minutes at 37°C. The beads were
then washed and resuspended in 45ul of 1X Quick Ligation buffer (New England Biolabs,
Ipswich, MA) and the NEBNext® adaptor for Illumina (New England Biolabs, Ipswich, MA). 5ul
of Quick T4 DNA ligase (New England Biolabs, Ipswich, MA) was added to the ligation mixture
and incubated at room temperature for 15 minutes (Figure 1 (5)).
The magnetic beads were then washed and resuspended in a 1X HotStart OneTaq®
PCR Master Mix (New England Biolabs, Ipswich, MA) containing 5ul of USER™' enzyme (New
England Biolabs, Ipswich, MA) and NEBNext® primers for Illumina (New England Biolabs,
Ipswich, MA). The PCR mixture was incubated at 37°C for 15 minutes and following PCR
cycling conditions is used: 95°C for 2 minutes followed by 25 cycles of 95°C for 30 seconds,
60°C for 30 seconds and 72°C for 1 minute (Figure 1 (6)). At the end of the 25 cycles, the PCR
mixture incubated at 72°C for 5 minutes. The PCR products obtained from the target
sequences were then sequenced using conventional methods.
Example 2: A variation on the method for enriching for target sequence for
sequencing with one target isolation probes.
The protocol in Example 1 and Figure 1 was followed through binding to streptavidin
beads (1)-(3) followed by steps shown in Figure 2A (7)-(11).
The beads were resuspended in a 50ul reaction mix containing 1X NEBuffer 4, 2.5 U
Exonuclease T and 2.5 U Exonuclease I and incubated for 10 minutes at 37°C (7).
The magnetic beads were washed and resuspended in 50ul of dA-Tailing reaction mix
and incubated for 30 minutes at 37°C. The beads were then washed and resuspended in 45ul
of 1X Quick Ligation and the NEBNext adaptor for Illumina. 5ul of Quick T4 DNA ligase was
added to the ligation mixture and incubated at room temperature for 15 minutes Figure 2A (8).
The magnetic beads were washed and resuspended in 50ul of 1X Exonuclease VII
buffer containing 20 units of Exonuclease VII (Epicentre, Madison, WI) and incubated for 10
minutes at 30°C (9). The enzyme was heat-inactivated following the manufacturer's protocol.
The beads were washed and resuspended in 50ul 1X NEBuffer 2 containing 15U T4 DNA
polymerase (New England Biolabs, Ipswich, MA) and 100uM dNTPs. The reaction was
incubated for 30 minutes at 20°C.

The beads were then washed and resuspended in 45ul of 1X Quick Ligation buffer and
the NEBNext adaptor for Illumina. 5ul of Quick T4 DNA ligase was added to the ligation
mixture and incubated at room temperature for 15 minutes (10).
USER cleavage of the adaptors and PCR amplification were performed as described in
Example 1.
Example 3: A method for enriching for target sequence for sequencing with one
Flap probe.
The protocol described in Example 1 was followed through ligation of the 3' adaptor
using a flap target isolation probe (see Figure 2B). The flap target isolation probe is
characterized by a single-stranded 3' region specific to the 5' end of the target sequence, an
internal biotin-dT, a 5' hairpin containing a cleavable dU, a NGS platform-specific sequencing
primer site, a library amplification primer site and a unique sample identifier sequence (1-3,12-
13). After ligation of the 3' adaptor, the beads were washed and resuspended in 50ul of 1X
REC Reaction Buffer 12 (Trevigen, Gaithersburg, MD) containing 5ul of 10X BSA additive
(Trevigen, Gaithersburg, MD) and 0.5 U Human Fen-1 (Trevigen, Gaithersburg, MD) and
incubated for 30 minutes at 30°C (14). The beads were then washed and resuspended in 45ul
of 1X Quick Ligation buffer and 5ul of Quick T4 DNA ligase and incubated at room temperature
for 15 minutes.
USER cleavage of the adaptors and PCR amplification were performed as described in
Example 1 (15).
Example 4: A variation on the method for enriching for target sequence for
sequencing with one target isolation probes.
The protocol in Example 1 was followed through single stranded 3' and 5' digestion
(Figure 1 (1)-(4) and Figure 2C (16)-(18)) using a target isolation probe with a 3'-
dideoxynucleotide. The beads were washed and resuspended in 45ul of 1X Quick Ligation
buffer and 10ul of 50uM 3' blunt-ended hairpin DNA adaptor and 5ul of Quick T4 DNA ligase
was added to the ligation mixture and incubated at room temperature for 15 minutes (16). The
З'adaptor sequence contained an NGS platform-specific sequencing primer site, a 5' phosphate
and a 3'-dideoxynucleotide.
After the beads were washed, the target/probe duplex was blunt ended, dA-tailed and
the 5' adaptor was ligated to the target, and the targets were amplified using the NEBNext Ultra
DNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina (New England Biolabs, Ipswich, MA), following the
manufacturers protocol for library preparation without size selection (17), (18).
Example 5: A method for enriching for target sequence for sequencing using a
target isolation probe and a random oligonucleotide.

Human gDNA (1ug) was sheared with a Covaris device following the manufacturer's
protocol for 500bp fragments (Figure 3 (19)). The sheared DNA was added to a 25ul
hybridization reaction mixture containing 20nmol of 3' target isolation probes, 50 bases in
length, specifically complementary to the 3' end of a 100bp-300bp nucleotide target sequence
within the 500bp gDNA fragment (Figure 3 (20)) using the technique described by Tiquia, et al.
(2004)). After hybridization, the 3' target isolation probe/target DNA duplexes were bound to
50ul of hydrophilic streptavidin beads for 30 minutes following the manufacturer's protocol
(Figure 3 (21)).
The beads were resuspended in a 50ul reaction mix containing 1X NEBuffer 4, 2.5 U
Exonuclease T and 2.5ul Exonuclease I and incubated for 10 minutes at 37°C (Figure 3 (22)).
The magnetic beads were washed and resuspended in 50ul of dA-Tailing reaction mix and
incubated for 30 minutes at 37°C. The beads were then washed and resuspended in 45ul of
1X Quick Ligation buffer and a 10ul of 50uM hairpin adaptor with a 3' T overhang containing a
cleavable nucleic acid base of dU and 5ul of Quick T4 DNA ligase was added to the ligation
mixture and incubated at room temperature for 15 minutes (Figure 3 (23)). The 3'adaptor
sequence contained an NGS platform-specific sequencing primer site, a library amplification
primer site and a unique strand identifier sequence, and a 3' dT-overhang.
After ligation, the beads were washed and resuspended in 50ul 1X NEBuffer 2
containing an additional 20nmol of random hexamer. The reaction was heated for 5 minutes at
95°C, then transferred to ice (Figure 3 (24)) before addition of 15 units Klenow (exo-) DNA
polymerase (New England Biolabs, Ipswich, MA) and 100uM dNTPs. The reaction was
incubated for 10 minutes at 20°C followed by 20 minutes at 37°C (Figure 3 (25)).
The beads were then washed and resuspended in 45ul of 1X Quick Ligation buffer (New
England Biolabs, Ipswich, MA) and a 5' single-strand hairpin adaptor containing a cleavable
nucleic acid base of dU and 5ul of Quick T4 DNA ligase (New England Biolabs, Ipswich, MA)
was added to the ligation mixture and incubated at room temperature for 15 minutes (Figure 3
(26)). The 5' adaptor sequence contained an NGS platform-specific sequencing primer site, a
library amplification site and a barcode sequence for sample identification.
The magnetic beads were then washed and resuspended in a 1X HotStart OneTaq
PCR Master Mix containing 5ul of USER enzyme and 2.5ul each of 10uM amplification primers
complementary to the 3' and 5' library amplification sites. The PCR mixture was incubated at
37°C for 15 minutes and following PCR cycling conditions is used: 95°C for 2 minutes followed
by 25 cycles of 95°C for 30 seconds, 60°C for 30 seconds and 72°C for 1 minute (Figure 3
(27)). At the end of the 25 cycles, the PCR mixture incubated at 72°C for 5 minutes. The PCR
products obtained from the target sequences were then sequenced using conventional
methods.

Example 6: A variation on the method for enriching for target sequence for
sequencing using target isolation probe and a second probe.
The protocol described in Example 5 was followed through ligation of the 3' adaptor
((19)-(23)). After ligation, the magnetic beads were washed and resuspended in 50ul of 1X
Exonuclease VII buffer with 20nmol of 5' target isolation probes, 50 bases in length,
complementary to the 5' end of the target sequences. The target isolation probes were
annealed to the targets by heating for 5 minutes at 95°C, followed by slowly cooling to 30°C
(Figure 4 (28)). 10 U of Exonuclease VII was added to the reaction and incubated for an
additional 10 minutes at 37°C (Figure 4 (29)). The enzyme was heat-inactivated following the
manufacturer's protocol. The beads were washed and resuspended in 50ul 1X NEBuffer 2
(New England Biolabs, Ipswich, MA) containing an additional 20nmol of 5' target isolation
probe. The reaction was heated for 5 minutes at 95°C, followed by slowly cooling to 30°C
before addition of 15 U T4 DNA polymerase (New England Biolabs, Ipswich, MA) and 100uM
dNTPs. The reaction was incubated for 30 minutes at 20°C.
After the beads were washed, ligation of the 5' adaptor, USER cleavage of the adaptors
and PCR amplification were performed as described in Example 4 using a hairpin adaptor with
a 3'-T overhang ((Figure 4 (30), (31)).
Example 7: A variation on the method for enriching for target sequence for
sequencing with two probes.
The protocol described in Example 4 was followed through 5' exonuclease digestion
and heat inactivation ((19)-(23), (28)-(29)) using 3' target isolation probes with an internal,
rather than a 3' biotin. After heat inactivation, the beads were washed and resuspended in 50ul
1X NEBuffer 2 containing 15 units Klenow (exo-) DNA polymerase and 100uM dNTPs. The
reaction was incubated for 10 minutes at 20°C followed by 20 minutes at 37°C (32).
After the beads were washed, ligation of the 5' adaptor, USER cleavage of the adaptors
and PCR amplification were performed as described in Example 5 ((26), (27)).
Example 8: A method for enriching for target sequence for sequencing with a
target isolation probe and a 5' flap probe.
The protocol described in Example 6 was followed through ligation of the 3' hairpin
adaptor (Figure 3, (19)-(23)). After ligation of the 3' adaptor, the beads were washed and
resuspended in 50ul of 1X REC Reaction Buffer 12 containing 20 nmol of flap 5' probe. The
flap probe consisted of a single-stranded 3'-region complementary to the 5' end of the target
and a 5' hairpin containing a cleavable dU, an NGS platform-specific sequencing primer site, a
library amplification primer site and a unique sample identifier sequence. The probe was
annealed to the 5' end of the target sequence by heating for 5 minutes at 95°C, followed by
slowly cooling to 30°C (35).

After annealing 5ul of 10X BSA additive and 0.5 units Human Fen-1 was added to
remove the 5' single stranded region and the reaction was incubated for 30 minutes at 30°C
(36). The beads were then washed and resuspended in 45ul of 1X Quick Ligation buffer and
5ul of Quick T4 DNA ligase for repairing the nick between the second strand of the flap probe
and the target DNA and incubated at room temperature for 15 minutes.
The magnetic beads were then washed and resuspended in a 1X HotStart OneTaq
PCR Master Mix containing 5ul of USER enzyme and amplification primers. The PCR mixture
was incubated at 37°C for 15 minutes and the following PCR cycling conditions were used:
95°C for 2 minutes followed by 25 cycles of 95°C for 30 seconds, 60°C for 30 seconds and
72°C for 1 minute. At the end of the 25 cycles, the PCR mixture incubated at 72°C for 5
minutes (37). The PCR products obtained from the target sequences were then sequenced
using conventional methods.
Example 9: A variation on the method for enriching for target sequence for
sequencing with two probes.
Human gDNA (1ug) was sheared with a Covaris following the manufacturer's protocol
for 500bp fragments (19). The sheared DNA was add to 25ul hybridization reaction containing
20nmol of 3' target isolation probes and 20nmol of 5' probes, each 50 bases in length and
specifying the 3' and 5' ends of 100 targets (38). After hybridization, the hybridized target
sequences were captured as described in example 2 (39).
The beads were resuspended in a 50ul reaction mix containing 1X NEBuffer 4, 2.5 units
Exonuclease T and 2.5ul Exonuclease I and incubated for 10 minutes at 37°C. The magnetic
beads were washed and resuspended in 50ul of 1X NEBuffer 2 containing 30 units of RecJf
(New England Biolabs, Ipswich, MA) and incubated for 10 minutes at 20°C (Figure 4).
The magnetic beads were washed and resuspended in 50ul of dA-Tailing reaction mix
and incubated for 30 minutes at 37°C. The beads were then washed and resuspended in 45ul
of 1X Quick Ligation buffer and the NEBNext adaptor for Illumina. 5ul of Quick T4 DNA ligase
was added to the ligation mixture and incubated at room temperature for 15 minutes (41).
USER cleavage of the adaptors and PCR amplification were performed as described in
Example 1 (42).

eval_task_config.task_instruction: Draft an English response to the U.S. Office Action.

scoring_policy.subjective_metrics: The Judge returns 0, 0.5, or 1 for each scored criterion using its own levels. G3-G5 additionally follow the synchronized zero-score rule below. The Judge does not calculate weights or totals.
scoring_policy.input_mode: Case source materials, task requirements, and the candidate response; no expert annotations or case-specific scoring layer.
scoring_policy.validation_checks: Case identity, input completeness, consultation of legal provisions, and verification of quotations are evaluation checks, not separately weighted criteria.

steps: Distribute the common-layer budget among applicable groups in the ratio foundation:amendment:argument = 25:20:55. If an entire group is not applicable, renormalize the remaining original group budgets.

Within the argument group, distribute its budget among applicable issue types according to argument_types.relative_weight. Inventive step is one complete issue type; its budget does not vary with the number of applicable inventive-step subcriteria.

Within each group other than argument, or within each argument issue type, distribute the budget among applicable criteria in proportion to each criterion's relative_weight. Use unrounded weights throughout the calculation.
weight_allocation.final_score: round(100 * C, 1), only when every applicable criterion is scored
weight_allocation.baseline_warning: The all-applicable percentages are illustrative only. Do not drop inapplicable entries from those percentages and renormalize the resulting flat list.
weight_allocation.calibration_note: These weights are initial design values, not proportions prescribed by the Word standard, and have not yet been calibrated against the new 100-case set.

applicability.amendment_rule: G3-G5 activate together when the candidate actually amends the claims and are scored using the Word levels. If the synchronized zero-score rule applies, all three remain active with score 0. Otherwise, when no amendment is made, all three are not_applicable.
applicability.argument_rule: Determine applicability of each G6 criterion from the complete OA, the actual points of dispute, the jurisdiction, and the necessary reasoning steps. A single inventive-step objection may require several subcriteria. A missing candidate response does not make an existing issue not applicable.
applicability.not_applicable: Use status=not_applicable and score=null only when a conditional criterion does not apply; provide the reason and references to source materials. Only not_applicable releases allocated weight.

amendment_zero_rule.trigger: The Judge determines that the claims should be amended, but the candidate OAR has not chosen an amendment strategy.
amendment_zero_rule.evidence_requirement: Each of G3-G5 must cite the case basis showing why amendment is needed and evidence that the candidate did not choose that strategy. A difference between pre_claim and post_claim alone is insufficient to infer that amendment is required.
amendment_zero_rule.defect_description_requirement: Each criterion's defect description must identify its current metric ID and explain that the zero score is required by this synchronized rule.
amendment_zero_rule.scope: Do not mark these three criteria not_applicable or redistribute the amendment budget. G2, G6, and all other scoring rules continue to apply as specified.

result_contract.scored: A score of 0, 0.5, or 1 and verifiable evidence references are required.
result_contract.unscored: not_applicable, not_evaluable, and failed require score=null. Conditional not_applicable results require a reason and source references.
result_contract.failure_handling: not_evaluable and failed retain their allocated shares and block the final score. Do not redistribute their shares to scored criteria or remove an inventive-step type because one subcriterion cannot be evaluated.
result_contract.consistency_checks: Validate required criteria, consistent applicability of G3-G5, compliance with the synchronized zero-score rule, and evidence fields. Programmatic checks do not replace semantic review.

audit_fields.common_group_allocation: Group budgets, active criteria, and argument.types with issue-type budgets and subcriteria.
audit_fields.common_allocated_weights: Allocated weights including shares reserved for not_evaluable or failed criteria.
audit_fields.common_effective_weights: Weights actually contributing to the score; not_applicable, not_evaluable, and failed have effective weight 0. Failed or unevaluable applicable criteria still block a final total.

scoring_policy.duplicate_defect_rule: Assign each minimal defect to one primary criterion rather than penalizing it repeatedly across criteria. The explicitly required synchronized G3-G5 zero scores are a policy exception; each must identify the current criterion and the reason for the rule-based zero score.

metrics.name: Accuracy of understanding the case facts and Office Action
metrics.evaluation_object: Whether the application, its current claims, the Office Action, and the relevant cited documents are correctly understood, and whether the validity of the grounds for objection is correctly assessed.

levels.1: Correctly understands the application, the claims, the technical features, and their relationships; accurately understands the meaning of the grounds for objection and accurately assesses whether they are valid.
levels.0.5: Correctly assesses the main technical solution, the grounds for objection, and the points open to argument, but has localized misunderstandings of noncritical facts, feature relationships, or document content; these do not change the main direction of the response and can be corrected locally.
levels.0: Misunderstands the technical solution of the application, feature relationships, or the Office Action; makes errors such as confusing the original claims, the current claims, and the proposed amended claims.

metrics.activation_condition: Required for every case.

metrics.name: Reasonableness of the overall response strategy
metrics.evaluation_object: Whether the choice between relying solely on argument and proactively amending the claims is reasonable; if proactive amendment is chosen, whether the choice of claims to amend is reasonable and whether any improper admissions are made.

levels.1: The choice of argument alone, amendment, or a combination of the two is supported by the case; the claims selected for treatment are appropriate, and the overall strategy addresses the core issues in the Office Action; no unsupported, materially adverse admissions are made.
levels.0.5: The main response approach is reasonable, but there are localized inappropriate choices in the treatment of noncore claims that do not affect the main position.
levels.0: The main response approach cannot address the core issues, for example, persisting with argument alone when the arguments lack a valid basis, or failing to include core claims requiring amendment in the strategy; makes adverse admissions that lack a basis in the Office Action and materially weaken the position on the main scope of protection.

metrics.activation_condition: Required for every case.

metrics.name: Effectiveness of claim amendments in addressing the issues identified in the Office Action [if amended]
metrics.evaluation_object: Whether the claim amendments themselves resolve the issues targeted by the Office Action, assessed separately from the quality of the response statement.

levels.1: The specific amendments correspond to the issues identified in the Office Action, and the amended claims, together with the response statement, are sufficient to overcome those defects.
levels.0.5: The amendments resolve the core defects identified in the Office Action, but the treatment of noncore defects is incomplete and requires localized correction.
levels.0: The core defects identified in the Office Action remain after amendment; or the amendments have no substantive connection to the defects identified in the Office Action.

metrics.activation_condition: G3-G5 activate together when the candidate actually amends the claims and are scored using the Word levels. If the synchronized zero-score rule applies, all three remain active with score 0. Otherwise, when no amendment is made, all three are not_applicable.

metrics.name: Proportionality of claim amendments and preservation of the scope of protection [if amended]
metrics.evaluation_object: Whether there is avoidable loss of protection while reasonably addressing the Office Action, assessed against the original protection objectives of the case.

levels.1: Added limitations, claim deletions, and other scope adjustments are reasonably necessary or reflect supported strategic tradeoffs; there is no unnecessary narrowing that can be clearly demonstrated from the case materials.
levels.0.5: There are individual unnecessary additional limitations or losses of noncore claims, but the main protection objectives of the original application are not materially affected; a less restrictive and equally reasonable localized adjustment can be specifically identified.
levels.0: Despite the existence of a supported, reasonable approach involving less narrowing, introduces significantly unnecessary limitations, deletes important claims, or abandons key protected subject matter, materially harming the main protection objectives.

metrics.activation_condition: G3-G5 activate together when the candidate actually amends the claims and are scored using the Word levels. If the synchronized zero-score rule applies, all three remain active with score 0. Otherwise, when no amendment is made, all three are not_applicable.

metrics.name: Legality and formal compliance of claim amendments [if amended]
metrics.evaluation_object: Whether amendments have a basis in the original disclosure and comply with amendment rules; whether clarity, support, antecedent basis, and claim dependencies meet the applicable requirements.

levels.1: The amended claim content and combinations have a verifiable basis in the original disclosure and comply with the applicable amendment rules; the amended claims are clear and supported by the description, with correct terminology, antecedent basis, and claim dependencies.
levels.0.5: The amendments have a basis in the original disclosure and the scope of protection can be determined, but there are correctable localized wording or citation-form defects; correction does not change the substantive technical solution.
levels.0: The amendments exceed the permissible scope, introduce content or combinations lacking a basis in the original disclosure, or create generalizations unsupported by the description; substantive errors in key wording, feature relationships, or claim dependencies make the scope of protection indeterminate or the technical solution untenable.

levels.1: Accepts or challenges the examiner's identification of the closest prior art on a supported basis; correctly identifies the specific differences between the claims and the closest prior art, correctly analyzes and defines the distinguishing technical features, and clearly and sufficiently performs the feature comparison needed to support that conclusion.
levels.0.5: Correctly identifies the closest prior art and the main distinguishing technical features, but some comparisons, feature relationships, or explanations of the supporting basis are incomplete; these can be supplemented using the existing materials.
levels.0: The identification of distinguishing technical features is untenable, or distinguishing technical features decisive to the conclusion are omitted; rejects the starting point for comparison without a basis; merely asserts that "differences exist" without substantively comparing the features at the core of the dispute.

3 NOVELTY (Art. 54 EPC)

3.1 Claim 1 is directed to a composition comprising a D-DT polypeptide for treating a subject, a tissue or an organ. The embodiment wherein a tissue or an organ is treated is interpreted as opposed to treating a subject as an in vitro treatment. This is also clear from the passage on p. 43, lines 17-19. In this case, the subject-matter is not entitled to the second medical use formulation of Art. 54(4) EPC and the claim is read as merely directed to the composition disregarding the intended use. For this reason, any document disclosing the D-DT protein, such as any of D4, D5 and D7, is novelty destroying for this embodiment of claim 1. The embodiment should be claimed separately as a method of treatment.

3.2 The present application does not meet the requirements of Article 52 (1) EPC because the subject-matter of claim 1 is not new in the sense of Article 54 (1) and (2) EPC.

4 INVENTIVE STEP (Art. 56 EPC)

4.1 Document D2 is considered to represent the most relevant state of the art and discloses a method of treating ischemia/reperfusion damage to a kidney in an individual comprising: administering to the individual one or more antibody molecules specific for one or more BMP-I isoforms (cl. 28), wherein the one or more antibody molecules to one or more BMP-I isoforms is administered systemically to the individual prior to an ischemia/reperfusion event (cl. 29). The subject-matter of claim 1 differs in that the compound is one of D-DT polypeptide or a recombinant D-DT polypeptide. No the technical effect could be identified from this difference.

The problem to be solved by the present invention may therefore be regarded as providing the provision of an alternative compound for treating or preventing ischemia-reperfusion. The proposed solution is one of D-DT polypeptide or a recombinant D-DT polypeptide.

This solution can be considered as involving an inventive step for the following reasons: D3 discloses the cardioprotective action of an agonist of MIF during ischemia and reperfusion and suggests that MIF receptor agonism by a small

molecule may provide protection against cardiac ischemic injury. Although MIF is a direct homologue of D-DT, there is no direct hint in the prior art that would link D-DT activity to ischemia protection instead of MIF.

Therefore, the proposed solution cannot be considered obvious and the claim is inventive.

4.2 In view of the lack of support (see 6.3), no inventive step can be acknowledged to the subject-matter of claim 2 or of its dependent claims 3-8.

5 UNPATENTABLE SUBJECT-MATTER (Art. 53 EPC)

5.1 Claim 8 refers to a method step comprising treating a subject. This falls under the exclusions from patentability contemplated in Art. 53(c) EPC. Hence, the claim should be deleted.

6 SUPPORT and DISCLOSURE (Art. 84, 83 EPC)

6.1 Claim 1 refers to a D-DT activator. This term does not fulfill the requirements of Articles 83 and 84 EPC. The term encompasses any agent having an effect anywhere upstream of the protein or gene. The claimed agent could modulate expression, be it directly or indirectly, or effect the function be it by direct interaction or indirectly. It would represent an undue burden to isolate and characterize all potential activators, without any effective pointer to their identity (Guidelines F-III,1) or to test every known compound and every conceivable future compound for the desired effect to see if it falls within the scope of the claims (Guidelines F-III, 9).

6.2 Claim 1 refers to an active D-DT polypeptide fragment. Neither the application or the prior art however discloses any example of an active D-DT fragment nor it provides sufficient indications about how to isolate such a fragment. Therefore, this embodiment is not considered sufficiently disclosed (Art. 83 EPC).

6.3 The application does not disclose a correlation between the endogenous expression or activity level of D-DT and the presence of an ischemia-reperfusion injury. Therefore claim 2 is not supported by the description (Art. 84 EPC). The post-published document D9 shows that a depletion of D-DT increases susceptibility to a stressful response to ischemia-reperfusion but not that low levels of D-DT can be used as a marker to detect an ongoing disorder. In other words, the susceptibility to a disease does not imply the presence of the disease itself. Therefore the disclosure of D9 cannot be used in support of the protection sought by claim 2.

7 CLARITY (Art. 84 EPC)

7.1 The expression in claim 1 "the composition for use comprising: administering..." is not clear (Art. 84 EPC) because it seems to define the composition by a method step. The claim should rather read "the composition comprising a D-DT polypeptide..." or even better "A composition comprising a D-DT polypeptide for use in a method of treating...".

8 CONCLUSIONS

8.1 The applicant is requested to file new claims which take account of the above comments.

8.2 When filing amended claims the applicant should at the same time bring the description into conformity with the amended claims. Care should be taken during revision, especially of the introductory portion and any statements of problem or advantage, not to add subject-matter which extends beyond the content of the application as originally filed (Article 123(2) EPC).

# Description — EP2643470A2

<!-- Applicant-filed description immediately before target OA 2014-09-09. No amendment requested by the target OA has been applied. -->

## Page 1

<!-- source: EP11842505_20120531.pdf; PDF page 2; source date 20120531 -->

TITLE OF THE INVENTION
Compositions and Methods for Diagnosing and Treating
Diseases and Disorders Associated with D-DT
5
BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION
Macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF) is the first cytokine
activity described and a key regulatory mediator that is released upon activation of
different cell types (Bloom, et al., 1966, Science 153:80-82; David, 1966, Proc Nati
Acad Sci USA 56:72-77; Bernhagen, et al., 2003, Nature 365:756-759). MIF
increases macrophage antimicrobial responses and it is expressed upstream of
cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-a, IFN-y, and IL-1B (Calandra, et al.,
2003 Nat Rev Immunol 3:791-800). MIF activates immune cells by binding to CD74,
leading to the recruitment of CD44 into a signaling complex, the stimulation of
15
nonreceptor tyrosine kinases, and initiation of the ERK1/2 MAP kinase pathway (Shi,
et al., 2006 Immunity 25:595-606; Leng, et al., 2003, J Exp Med 197:1467-1476).
The chemokine receptors CXCR2 and CXCR4 also become activated by MIF via
noncognate interactions that are reinforced in the presence of CD74 (Bernhagen, et
al., 2007, Nat Med 13:587-596). Among mesenchymal cell types, MIF binding to
cardiomyocyte CD74 stimulates the AMP-activated kinase (AMPK) cascade to
mediate protection from ischemic injury (Miller, et al., 2008, Nature 451:578-582;
Qi, et al., 2009, J Clin Invest 119: 3807-3816).
Although MIF receptor knockout mice (CD74-1-) phenocopy features
MIF deficiency (Meyer-Siegler, et al., 2006, J Immunol 177:8730-8739; Topilski, et
25
al., 2002, J Immunol 168:1610-1617), recent observations have led to the hypothesis
that there may be a second ligand for CD74. MIF-deficient B cells, for example, are
more sensitive to apoptosis than wild-type B cells, but the magnitude of this defect is
twofold more pronounced in CD74-deficient cells (Gore, et al., 2008, J Biol Chem
283:2784-2792). Intravital microscopy studies also have shown a more pronounced
30
effect of antagonisı of CD74 than MIF in monocyte arrest (Bernhagen, et al., 2007,
Nat Med 13:587-596). Anti-MIF antibodies, although highly effective in
experimental studies, do not completely inhibit CD74-dependent cellular activation
responses (Chagnon, et al., 2005, Ciro Res 96:1095-1102).


## Page 2

<!-- source: EP11842505_20140807.pdf; PDF page 1; source date 20140807 -->

D-dopachrome tautomerase (D-DT) (also known as MIF-2) and MIF
show a conserved intron-exon structure and their coding regions are highly
homologous. The genes for MIF and D-DT are in close apposition to each other and
to two theta-class glutathione S-transferases, suggesting that these gene clusters arose
by an ancestral duplication event. D-DT was named for its ability to tautomerize the
nonnaturally occurring, D-stereoisomer of dopachrome, which is a catalytic property
shared with MIF. This activity has been hypothesized to be a vestigial function that
reflects MIF's ancestral origin in the invertebrate melanotic encapsulation response
(Fingerle-Rowson, et al., 2009, Mol Cell Biol 29:1922-1932). A crystal structure of
D-DT has verified its 3D similarity with MIF (Sugimoto, et al., 1999, Biochemistry
38:3268-3279). With the exception of recent studies indicating an interaction between
the MIF and D-DT genes in the expression of proangiogenic factors and COX-2 in
adenocarcinoma cell lines (Xin, et al., 2010, Mol Cancer Res 8:1601-1609; Coleman,
et al., 2008, J Immunol 181:2330-2337), there have been no studies of the biologic
functions of D-DT.


## Page 2a

<!-- source: EP11842505_20140807.pdf; PDF page 2; source date 20140807 -->


JP 2009178073 provides a method for the detection of abnormal fat accumulation including
determining the expression quantity of D-dopachrome tautomerase (DDT) in a sample derived from a
living body, a reagent for the detection of abnormal fat accumulation, a method for screening an
antiobesic substance and an agent for the treatment or prevention of obesity containing DDT or a
nucleic acid encoding DDT as an active component.
WO2008/011193 discloses uses of BMP-1 isoforms for diagnosing and treating defects and disorders
of bone and soft tissues. Also described is a newly isolated variant of the BMP-1 isoform BMP-1-3.
"Limiting Cardiac Ischemic Injury by Augmenting the MIF-AMPK Signaling Cascade with a Novel Class
of MIF Receptor Agonists" (Wang et al., Circulation, vol. 21, Suppl. S, 23 November 2010, page
A15835) discloses that MIF receptor agonism by a small molecule approach offers protection against
cardiac ischemic injury by augmenting the MIF-AMPK signaling pathway.
"Cooperative regulation of non-small cell lung carcinoma angiogenic potential by macrophage
migration inhibitory factor and its homolog, D-dopachrome tautomerase" (Coleman et al, The Journal
Of Immunology, vol. 181, no. 4, 1 August 2008, pages 2330-2337 - already mentioned above)
discloses D-DT's synergism with MIF and suggests that the combined therapeutic targeting of both
family members may enhance current anti-MIF-based therapies.
"Cooperative regulation of non-small cell lung carcinoma angiogenic potential by macrophage
migration inhibitory factor and its homolog, D-dopachrome tautomerase" (Merk et al, Inflammation
Research, vol. 59, no. Suppl. 1, March 2010, pages s120-s121) discloses that D-DT mediates
inflammation, activates similar pro-inflammatory pathways and mediates lethal shock.


## Page 2 (continued)

Despite the advances made in the art for detecting and treating
inflammation associated with MIF signaling through CD74, there is a need in the art
for the detection and treatment of inflammation associated with other molecules that
signal through CD74. The present invention fulfills these needs.
SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION
The present invention relates to the discovery that altered levels of D-
DT (also known as MIF-2) are associated with disorders and diseases. Thus, the
present invention relates to compositions and methods useful for the assessment,
diagnosis, characterization, prevention and treatment of disorders and diseases
associated with an elevated level of D-DT. The present invention also relates to
compositions and methods useful of the assessment, diagnosis, characterization,
prevention and treatment of disorders and diseases associated with a reduced level of
D-DT.
In one embodiment, the invention is a method of diagnosing a disease
or disorder in a subject including the steps of: determining the level of D-DT in a
biological sample from the subject, comparing the level of D-DT in the biological
sample with a comparator control, and diagnosing the subject with a disease or
disorder when the level of D-DT in the biological sample is different than the level of



## Page 3

<!-- source: EP11842505_20120531.pdf; PDF page 4; source date 20120531 -->

D-DT of the comparator control. In one embodiment, the level of D-DT in the
biological sample is elevated when compared with the comparator control, while in
another embodiment, the level of D-DT in the biological sample is reduced when
compared with the comparator control. In one embodiment, the level of D-DT in the
biological sample is determined by measuring the level of D-DT mRNA, while in
another embodiment, the level of the level of D-DT in the biological sample is
determined by measuring the level of D-DT polypeptide. In some embodiments, the
level of D-DT in the biological sample is determined by measuring an enzymatic
activity of D-DT polypeptide in the biological sample. In another embodiment, the
level of D-DT in the biological sample is determined by measuring the binding of a
detectable molecule to the D-DT enzyme substrate binding site. In a further
embodiment, the level of D-DT in the biological sample is determined by measuring
the displacement of a detectable molecule from the D-DT enzyme substrate binding
site. In various embodiments, the comparator control is at least one selected from the
group consisting of: a positive control, a negative control, a historical control, a
historical norm, or the level of a reference molecule in the biological sample. In a
particular embodiment, the reference molecule is MIF. The method of diagnosing a
disease or disorder of the present invention useful in diagnosing a varicty of diseases
and disorders associated with D-DT, including, for example, infection, inflammatory
disease, autoimmunity, cancer and ischemia-reperfusion injury. In preferred
embodiments, the subject is human.

DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION
The present invention relates to the discovery that altered levels of D-
DT (also known as MIF-2) are associated with disorders and diseases. Thus, the
present invention relates to compositions and methods usefu for the assessment,
diagnosis, characterization, prevention and treatment of disorders and diseases
associated with an elevated level of D-DT. The present invention also relates to
compositions and methods useful of the assessment, diagnosis, characterization,
prevention and treatment of disorders and diseases associated with a reduced level of
D-DT.

amplified segment of the desired farget sequence, The length of the amplified segment
of the desired target sequence is determined by the relative positions of the primers
with respect to each other, and therefore, this length is a controllable parameter. By
virtue of the repeating aspect of the process, the method is referred to as the
"polymerase chain reaction" (hereinafter "PCR"). Because the desired amplified
segments of the target sequence becomne the predominant sequences (in terms of
concentration) in the mixture, they are said to be "PCR amplified". As used herein,

Example 1: The D-dopachrome fautomerase (D-DT) gene product is a cytokine and
functional homolog of macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIlF)
The functional characterization of human and mouse D-DT (also
known as MIF-2) is described herein. Recombinant D-DT was produced and was
demonstrated to bind with high affinity to CD74, activate the ERK1/2 MAP kinase
signaling cascade, and recapitulate many of the inflammatory functions of MilF,
including modulation of macrophage migration and glucocorticoidinduced
immunosuppression. The administration of an anti-D-DT antibody, like anti-MIF,
protects mice from lethal endotoxic shock by reducing the circulating levels of
proinflammatory cytokines (TNF-a, IFN-y, IL-12p70, and IL-IB) and increasing the
circulating concentration of the anti-inflammatory cytokine, IL-10. An analysis of
clinical samples from patients with sepsis or cancer also revealed that D-DT is
systemically expressed and that circulating levels correlate with MIF and with the
severity of inflammatory disease and malignancy.
Both mouse and human D-DT proteins show conservation in their
catalytic, N-terminal proline but they lack MIF's -CXXC- and pseudo(E)LRmotifs,
the latter of which is known to mediate noncognate interactions with CXCR2 and
CXCR4 (Bernhagen, et al., 2007, Nat Med 13:587-596; Weber, et al., 2008, Proc Nati
Acad Sci USA 105: 16278-16283). As described herein, a recombinant, endotoxin-
free D-DT protein was produced and it is shown that D-DT, like MIF, tautomerizes


## Page 61

<!-- source: EP11842505_20120531.pdf; PDF page 62; source date 20120531 -->

the model substrate, p-hydroxyphenylpyruvate, albeit the measured velocity is ~10
times lower than that analyzed for MIF. D-DT is constitutively expressed in different
tissues and it is up-regulated by proinflammatory activation. MIF is known to bind to
the type Il transmembrane protein, CD74, leading to its intracellular phosphorylation,
5
the recruitment of the coreceptor CD44, and the activation of SRC family kinases and
the ERK1/2 MAPK pathivay (Shii, et al., 2006 Immunity 25:595-606; Leng, et al.,
2003, J Exp Med 197:1467-1476). Although the interaction between D-DT and
sCD74 was reduced in comparison with MIF when measured by both competition
binding and BIAcore studies, the ERK1/2 activation potential of D-DT and MIF
appeared comparable by Western blotting, The KD of sCD74 for D-DT was 60% of
that measured for MIF; D-DT was found to have an ~3-fold higher association rate
(ka) to sCD74 but to dissociate (kd) ~11-fold faster than MIF. Although not wishing
to be bound by any particular theory, these differences in association and dissociation
values may differentiate the signaling action of the two proteins; e.g., D-DT binding
to the receptor might not always trigger a signaling cascade but might result in its
internalization. MIF showed a steeper dose response than D-DT in measurements of'
macrophage migration inhibition and glucocorticoid overriding, but the resolution of'
these cell-based assays may be too limited to make precise, quantitative conclusions.
These results may support the notion that D-DT is a less potent cytokine that might be
associated with the dowi-regulation of inflammation.
As described herein, anti-D-DT antibodies were produced that do not
cross-react with MIF; these antibodies allowed for measurements of this protein in
biologic specimens, D-DT' was expressed in the serum of endotoxemic mice at levels
that were ~60% those of MIF. MIF is a high, upstream mediator of septic shock, and
immunoneutralization, genetic deletion, or pharmacologic inhibition of MIF protects
from lethal shock induced by different microbial pathogens, even when administered
many hours after microbial invasion (Bernhagen, et al., 1993, Nature 365:756-759;
Bozza, et al., 1999, J Exp Med 189:341-346; Calandra, et al., 1998, Proc Natl Acad
Sci USA 95:11383-11388; Arjona, et al., 2007, J Clin Invest 117: 3059-3066;
McDevitt, et al., 2006, J Exp Med 203:1185-1196). Immunoneutralization of D-DT
conferred protection from lethal endotoxemia and this effect was accompanied by a
broad reduction in the systemic expression of TNF-0, IL-IB, IL-12p70, and IFN-y and
an increase in the circulating levels of the anti-inflammatory mediator, IL-10. Given

<!-- source: EP11842505_20120531.pdf; PDF page 63; source date 20120531 -->

current development of MIF inhibitors for the treatment of the inflammatory diseases
(Arjona, et al., 2007, J Clin Invest 1|7: 3059-3066; Lolis, et al., 2003, Nat Rev Drug
Discov 2:635-645; Cournia, el al. 2009, J Med Chem 52:416-424), it sas also of
interest to determine whether the combined neutralization of MIF and D-DT had a
synergistic effect. MIF levels are elevated in patients with systemic inflammatory
disease or with neoplasia, and in many instances a correlation between disease
severity and MIF levels has been observed (Grieb, et al., 2010, Drug News Perspect
23:257-264). Like MIF, D-DT circulates at baseline levels in healthy individuals and
there is a correlation in the plasma concentrations of the two mediators. Circulating
D-DT levels increase significantly in patients with sepsis or ovarian cancer and show
a strong correlation with MIF, consistent with the explanation that the two mediators
may be coordinately expressed in response to similar activating stimuli. The findings
described herein include that D-DT is a close structural and functional homolog of'
MIF, that it binds and activates the MIF receptor, and that targeting D-DT, similar to
MIF, protects mice from lethal endotoxemia.
Like MIF (Bacher, et al., 1997, Am J Pathol 150:235-246), D-DT was
found to be widely expressed in tissues, As described elsewhere herein, macrophages
produce 20-fold more MIF than D-DT in response to LPS, consistent with the
explanation that there may be cell-specific release of these mediators and that in
contrast to MIF, nonmacrophage sources of D-DT contribute more importantly to the

and AP-1 binding elements (alggen.Isi.upc.es). Of note, the human D-DT gene lacks

264). Although not wishing to be bound by any particular theory, one difference

Cloning and Purification of D-DT Protein
The cDNAs for the human and mouse D-DT proteins were prepared by
amplification of mRNA from human or murine monocytes and subcloned into the
pET22b expression vector. For native protein expression, a stop codon was
engineered. Bacterial extract was purified using a Q Sepharose column (Amersham)
and subsequent HPLC using a C18 column (Amersham). D-DT was refolded using
the protocol established for MIF renaturation (Bernhagen, et al., 1994, Biochemistry
33: 14144-14155). Protein purity was verified by Coomassie and fidelity confirmed
by mass spectroscopy. The resulting proteins contained <1 pg LPS/ug protein as
quantified by the PyroGene Recombinant Factor C assay (Cambrex). MIF proteins
were produced as described carlier (Bernhagen, et al., 1994, Biochemistry 33: 14144-
14155). D-dopachrome tautomerase activity was assessed using the substrate HPP,
measuring the change in absorbance at 306 nm for 180 s (Stamps, et al., Biochemistry
39:9671-9678).

Polyclonal antibodies against recombinant mouse or human D-DT
were produced in rabbits, IgO antibody fractions were isolated by Protein A agarose
affinity chromatography (Pierce) and sterile filtered. Microtiter plates (Nunc) were
coated with 15 ug/mL of polyclonal anti-D-DT, washed, and blocked in 1% BSA and
1% sucrose. Samples were added and incubated for 2 hours, followed by biotinylated

after LPS challenge, and serum cytokines were analyzed by Luminex (Bio-Rad).
Patient Samples
Serum concentrations of D-DT and MIF were measured in 85 healthy
individuals and in 37 septic patients hospitalized in the medical intensive care unit
(Lesur, et al., 2010, Crit Care 14:R131). The median APACHE II score at the time of
intensive care unit admission was 22 points (range: 10-36 points). The mortality rate
was 27%. The etiologic agents of sepsis vere Gram-negative bacteria (43%) and
Gram-positive bacteria (49%). Tivo patients had an infection with Grampositive and
Gram-negative bacteria and one with fungi. Sera from women with biopsy-proven
ovarian cancer (n = 21) were from Yale-New Haven Hospital.
The results of this example are now described.
Purification and Characterization of the D-DT Protein
The genes for MIF and D-DT lie within O.1 kb of each other in both
the mouse and human genomes and have a similar organizational relationship with
nearby genes for matrix metalloproteinase 11 and two theta class GSTs (Figure 1).
The amino acid sequences show 34% identity between human MIF and human D-DT
and 27% identity between murine MIF and murine D-DT. The D-DT proteins share
with MIF a canonical N-terminal proline (formed after posttranslational excision of
the initiating methionine), which catalyzes substrate fautomerization (Bendrat, et al.,
1997, Biochemistry 36:15356-15362), but they lack two of the three conserved
cysteines (Cys59 and Cys80) that appear in all known mammalian MIF proteins.
Murine and human D-DT also lack the pseudo(E)LR (Argl1, Asp44) motif that
mediates MIF's noncanonical interactions with the CXCR2 chemokine receptor
(Weber, et al., 2008, Proc Natl Acad Sci USA 105: 16278-16283). The mRNA for D-
DT does not encode either an N-terminal or an internal secretory signal sequence,
suggesting that like MIF, D-DT is secreted by a specialized, nonclassical export
pathway (Merk, et al., 2009, J Immunol 182:6896-6906).


## Page 67

<!-- source: EP11842505_20120531.pdf; PDF page 68; source date 20120531 -->

The cDNAs for human and mouse D-DT were prepared from
monocytes and cloned into a bacterial expression vector for recombinant protein
production. Work was performed with native sequence proteins because structure-
function studies have shown that modifications of the N or C termini interfere with
5
trimer formation, the functional unit of'MIF (Bendrat, et al., 1997, Biochemistry
36:15356-15362; Sun, et al., 1996, Proc Natl Acad Sci USA 93: 5191-5196; BI-Turk,
et al., 2008, Biochemistry 47:10740-10756). Recombinant D-DT protein was purified
by anion exchange chromatography followed by high performance liquid
chromatography (HPLC) (Figure 2A). Mass spectroscopy of purified mouse D-DT
protein gave an m/z of 12,947, which lies within 0.02% of the calculated mass for D-
DT (Figure 2B). A minor peak of 13,079 Da also was detected; this peak corresponds
to the molecular mass of D-DT with an uncleaved N-terminal methionine (expected
m/z = 13,077). MIF tautomerizes model substrates such as D-dopachrome and p-
hydoxyphenylpyruvate (HPP) (whether a physiological substrate exists is unknown)
(Fingerle-Rowson, et al., 2009, Mol Cell Biol 29:1922-1932), and D-DT purified
from liver has tautomerization activity (Rosengren, et al., 1996, Mol Med 2:143-149;
Odh, et al., 1993, Biochem Biophys Res Commun 197:619-624). It was verified that
recombinant D-DT tautomerizes HPP with a specific activity that is ~10 times lower
than that measured for MIF (D-DT = 0.5 ‡ 0.1 4306 min-1 uM-1, and MIF = 4.3 +
1.1 4306 min-1 4M-1, P <0.001) (Figure 2C). A possible explanation for the
discrepancy inactivity might be structural differences in the active site regions of D-
DT and MIF, r'esulting in a reduced affinity of D-DT to its substrate (Sugimoto, et al.,
1999, Biochemistry 38:3268-3279; Sun, et al.,1996, Proe Natl Acad Sci USA 93:
5191-5196). A polyclonal anti-D-DT antibody was prepared to establish an ELISA.
This antibody recognized both murine and human D-DT but did not cross-react with
MIF in its denatured form (assessed by Western blot; Figure 2D, Left) or in its native
form (assessed by BLISA; Figure 2D, Right).
D-DT Binds the MIF Receptor, CD74, and the Intracellular Protein, JAB1
MIF activates ERK1/2 phosphorylation by engaging CD74, and a high-
affinity binding interaction between MIF and the CD74 ectodomain (CD7473-232 or
sCD74) has been demonstrated by surface plasmon resonance (Leng, ct al., 2003, J
Exp Med 197:1467-1476). The interaction between D-DT and sCD74 in a
competition binding assay was studied. D-DT reduced MIF binding to the CD74


## Page 68

<!-- source: EP11842505_20120531.pdf; PDF page 69; source date 20120531 -->

ectodomain in a dose-dependent manner, with a maximal effect of ~50% compared
with MIF (Figure 3A). Measurement of the equilibrium dissociation constants
between human D-DT or MIF and sCD74 by surface plasmon resonance (BIAcore
analysis) revealed a high-affinity binding interaction between D-DT and the MIF
receptor (KD of 5.42 × 10-9 M) (Figure 3B), albeit 60% lower than for MIF (KD =
1.40 × 10-9 M). Detailed analysis revealed a ka of 1.2 × 105 M-I's-1 for D-DT and
only 4.3 × 104 M-1's-1 for MIF, whereas the dissociation rate (kd) was 11-fold
lower for MIF than for D-DT (6 x 10-5's-1 and 6.6 x 10-4's1, respectively). These
measurements demonstrate that D-DT has an ~3-fold higher binding rate to the
receptor CD74, but also dissociates much faster than MIF. The intracellular
transcriptional regulator and COP9 signalosome component JABI is a well
characterized binding partner of MIF that has been implicated in MIF-dependent
control of cell proliferation (Kleemann, et al., 2000, Nature 408:211-216). D-DT
binds to JABI as demonstrated by coimmunoprecipation (Figure 3C), and the
interaction affinity between JAB1 and D-DT appears comparable to that observed
betveen JABI and MIF.
Differential Expression of D-DT and MIF
The differential expression of D-DT in tissue compared with MIF was
assessed. Esumi et al. have published Northern blotting data for D-DT expression that
suggest enhanced expression in the murine brain compared with Mif (Esumi, et al.,
1998, Mamm Genome 9:753-757). Eight different mouse organs were analyzed by
Western blotting for D-DT, MIF, and CD74. D-DT and MIF were present in
constitutive and appreciable levels in all tissues examined, with the greatest difference
observed in the testis, where D-DT appeared in severalfold higher concentrations
compared with MIF (Figure 3D). Immunostaining of murine tissue confirmed these
results and showed that D-DT, like MIF (Bacher, et al., 1997, Am J Pathol 150:235-
246), is detected in virtually all cells, with prominent staining in the epithelia of the
kidney, the lung, the bowel, hepatocytes, and the follicular area of the spleen (Figure
3Е).
D-DT Initiates ERK-1/2 Phosphorylation in a MIF Receptor-Complex-
Dependent Manner, Mediates Macrophage Migration Arrest, and
Counterregulates Glucocorticoid-Induced Immunosuppression


## Page 69

<!-- source: EP11842505_20120531.pdf; PDF page 70; source date 20120531 -->

MIF binding to CD74 leads to the recruitment of CD44 and the
intracellular phosphorylation of' these proteins, resulting in the activation of SRC
family nonreceptor tyrosine kinases and the initiation of the ERK1/2 MAP kinase
cascade (Shi, et al., 2006 Immunity 25:595-606; Leng, et al., 2003, J Exp Med
197:1467-1476). Stimulation of cultured macrophages with increasing concentrations
of recombinant D-DT produced a dose-dependent phosphorylation of ERK1/2, with
an activating effect that was both sustained (2 h) (Mitchell, et al., 1999, J Biol Chem
274:18100-18106) and comparable to that observed for MIF (Figure 4A, Top).
Costimulation with D-DT and MIF revealed an additive effect of the two proteins in
the ERK1/2 MAP kinase pathway (Figure 4A, Middle). D-DT-induced ERK1/2
phosphorylation was strictly dependent on the expression of both CD74 and CD44, as
previously reported for MIF (Shi, et al., 2006 Immunity 25:595-606) (Figure 4A,
Bottom).
The biologic activity of recombinant D-DT was analyzed by first
assaying for MIF's effect on macrophage chemotaxis (Hermanowski-Vosatka, et
al.,1999, Biochemistry 38:12841-12849). D-DT inhibited chemotaxis induced by
CCL2/monocyte chemotactic protein (MCP)-I, but with a less steep dose response
and reduced inhibitory action at 1 ug/mL compared with MIF (Figure 4B). Aithough
not wishing to be bound by any particular theory, this observation may be explained
by the reduced binding affinity of D-DT for the MIF receptor or different rates of
ligand association/dissociation and a consequent reduction in the downstream events
necessary for CCL2 desensitization. MIF is unique among immune mediators in its
ability to counterregulate the immunosuppressive action of glucocorticoids, which
occurs via intracellular pathways that involve cytoplasmic phospholipase A2, IkB1,
and MKP-1 (Calandra, et al., 1995, Nature 377:68-71; Flaster, et al, 2007, Mol
Endocrinol 21:1267-1280; Roger, et al., 2005, Eur J Immunol 35:3405-3413). Using
a standardized assay (Calandra, et al., 1995, Nature 377:68-71), it was further
observed that D-DT, like MIF, counterregulated the inhibitory effect of
glucocorticoids on TNF production from lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-stimulated
macrophages (Figure 4C). Similar to observations in the migration assay, D-DT
shows a decreased counterregulatory potential at low concentrations compared with
MIF, which may be attributed to lower binding affinity to the MIF receptor:
D-DT Is Produced in Response to LPS and Mediates Lethal Endotoxemia


## Page 70

<!-- source: EP11842505_20120531.pdf; PDF page 71; source date 20120531 -->

Whereas macrophages have been considered historically to be a main
target of MIF action, these cells also are a major source of MIF production in
response to microbial products and tissue invasion in vivo (Calandra, et al, 1994, J
Exp Med 179:1895-1902). Cultured macrophages were stimulated with 1 Jg/mL of
5
Escherichia coli LPS and the secretion of D-DT and MIF was quantified by specific
ELISA. LPS-stimulated macrophages released D-DT into conditioned medium with
kinetics that were very similar to those of MIF (Figure 5A). Peak levels were
detectable at 16 hours and decreased thereafter. Unstimulated cells also slowly
released these proteins into supernatants, which in the case of MIF has been attributed
to a low level of constitutive secretion (Merk, et al., 2009, J Immunol 182:6896-
6906).
It was next assessed whether there is reciprocal regulation of D-DT
and MIF expression in macrophages. D-DT or MIF were depleted in immortalized
macrophages by siRNA-mediated knockdown but detected no effect on the expression
level of the reciprocal protein in response to LPS stimulation (Figure 5B). The
administration of LPS to mice resulted in a timedependent increase in plasma D-DT
concentrations (6.0 ‡ 4.3 ng/mL 1o 26 ‡ 12 ng/mL at 24 h), and this increase
mimicked the rise observed for MIF (1.0 = 0.9 ng/mL to 43 ‡. 28 ng/mL at 24 h)
(Figure SC). D-DT also is detectable in plasma under basal conditions and at
comparable levels to MIF (D-DT = 6.0 ‡ 4.3 ng/mL and MIF = 1.0 + 0.9 ng/ml)
(Calandra, et al., 1995, Nature 377:68-71). It is noteworthy that whereas plasma Milf
and D-DT circulate in similar concentrations under basal or stimulated conditions,
LPS-stimulated macrophages produce 20-fold more MIF than D-DT (Figure 5A).
Although not wishing to be bound by any particular theory, this observation is
consistent with the explanation that nonmacrophage sources of D-DT contribute
significantly to plasma D-DT expression in vivo.
Immmunoneutralization of D-DT Protects from Lethal Endotoxemia
Immmunoneutralization or genetic deletion of MIF protects mice from
endotoxic shock (Bernhagen, et al., 1993, Nature 365:756-759; Bozza, et al., 1999, J
Exp Med 189:341-346) and subsequent studies demonstrated that this protective
effect is due to a reduction in the expression of tissue-damaging, effector cytokines
such as TNF and IL-1 (Mitchell, et al., 2002, Proc Natl Acad Sci USA 99:345-350;
Calandra, et al., 2000, Nat Med 6:164-170). The administration of' a specific anti-D-


## Page 71

<!-- source: EP11842505_20120531.pdf; PDF page 72; source date 20120531 -->

DT antibody before the injection of an LD80 dose of LPS increased survival from 20
to 79% (Figure SD), which is a level of protection comparable to that of anti-MIF
(Bernhagen, et al., 1993, Nature 365:756-759). An analysis of plasma cytokine
expression showed that D-DT neutralization was associated with a significant
5
reduction in the circulating concentration of several proinflammatory cytokines (TNF-
a, IL-IB, IFN-y, and IL-12p70) implicated in shock pathogenesis (Figure SE). In
contrast, the concentration of the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10 was increased in
the anti-D-DT-treated group compared with controls.
D-DT Expression Is Up-Regulated in Patients with Sepsis, Invasive
Cancer, or Vasculitis
To determine whether D-DT is up-regulated in human disease and to
assess potential relationships between D-DT and MIF production in vivo, the serum
concentrations of these mediators were analyzed in individuals with sepsis or with
ovarian cancer, which are two conditions characterized by high levels of MIF in
plasma (Calandra, et al., 2000, Nat Med 6:164-170; Visintin, et al., 2008, Clin
Cancer Res 14:1065-1072). There was a statistically significant increase in
circulating D-DT protein in patients with sepsis compared with healthy controls
(sepsis patients, 55.5 ‡ 61.3 ng/mL; control group, 5.9 ‡ 3.9 ng/mL; P < 0.0001)
(Figure 6A). MIF levels also were elevated, as expected from prior work (Calandra, et
al., 2000, Nat Med 6:164-170; Bozza, et al., 2004, Shock 22:309-313; Lehmann, et
al., 2001, Intensive Care Med 27:1412-1415) (sepsis patients, 111.0 + 69.0 ng/mL;
control group, 6.3 ‡ 6.2 ng/mL; P < 0.0001). Receiver operator characteristic (ROC)
analysis revealed an area under the curve of 0.99 for MIF or D-DT, indicating that
both proteins show excellent sensitivity and specificity for the diagnosis of sepsis.
These measurements further revealed that serum levels of D-DT, like MIF (Bozza, et
al., 2004, Shock 22:309-313; Emonts, et al., 2007, Clin Infect Dis 44:1321-1328),
correlate with disease severity as determined by APACHE I clinical severity scores
(Figure 6B). Both D-DT and MIF show a significant association with outcome
parameters; however, a more precise assessment of the prognostic value of these
proteins may be obtained by serial measurements. Serum D-DT and MIF
concentrations also correlate in healthy individuals, and the correlation coefficient
increases from R = 0.32 to R = 0.5 for the analysis of these mediators in patients with
sepsis (Figure 6C). Circulating D-DT concentrations were also found to be elevated


## Page 72

<!-- source: EP11842505_20120531.pdf; PDF page 73; source date 20120531 -->

in patients with ovarian cancer (cancer patients, 15.2 ‡ 13.8 ng/mL; control group, 5.9
‡3.9 ng/mL; P < 0.0001) (Figure 6D), ROC analysis revealed an area under the curve
of 0.8, which is comparable to that observed for MIF (0.7). The correlation between
MIF and D-DT serum concentrations was stronger and showed greater statistical
5
significance than that observed for septic patients (R = 0.9, P = 0.0001). D-DT
expression is up-regulated in subjects with vasculitis and D-DT concentrations
correlate with MIF and the presence of vasculitis (Figure 7).
Example 2: Ischemia-reperfusion injury
As described herein, D-DT activates the cardioprotective AMPK
pathway in rat heart muscles, Mouse recombinant DDT activates AMP-activated
protein kinase in rat heart left ventricular papillary muscles. DDT incubation leads to
phosphorylation of threonine 172, the major activating site in the catalytic alpha
subunit of AMPK, as well as downstream target acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC).
AMPK pathway activation by DDT is dose and time dependent (Figures 8 and 9).
Moreover, endogenous DDT has a role in mediating AMPK activation
during hypoxia in isolated rat heart left ventricular muscles (Figure 9). The addition of
purified rabbit polyclonal neutralizing D-DT antibody for 30 minutes prior to and
during 15 minutes of hypoxia significantly reduced the critical phosphorylation of
threonine 172 in the activating domain of the alpha catalytic subunit of AMP-
activated protein kinase. DDT antibody also decreased the phosphorylation of
downstream acetyl-CoA carboxylase. Control was performed with non-immune IgG
incubation. Figure 9B shows a comparison to incubation with MIF neutralizing
antibody. p = 0.05.

scoring_policy.subjective_metrics: The Judge returns 0, 0.5, or 1 for each scored criterion using its own levels. G3-G5 additionally follow the synchronized zero-score rule below. The Judge does not calculate weights or totals.
scoring_policy.input_mode: Case source materials, task requirements, and the candidate response; no expert annotations or case-specific scoring layer.
scoring_policy.validation_checks: Case identity, input completeness, consultation of legal provisions, and verification of quotations are evaluation checks, not separately weighted criteria.

steps: Distribute the common-layer budget among applicable groups in the ratio foundation:amendment:argument = 25:20:55. If an entire group is not applicable, renormalize the remaining original group budgets.

Within the argument group, distribute its budget among applicable issue types according to argument_types.relative_weight. Inventive step is one complete issue type; its budget does not vary with the number of applicable inventive-step subcriteria.

Within each group other than argument, or within each argument issue type, distribute the budget among applicable criteria in proportion to each criterion's relative_weight. Use unrounded weights throughout the calculation.
weight_allocation.final_score: round(100 * C, 1), only when every applicable criterion is scored
weight_allocation.baseline_warning: The all-applicable percentages are illustrative only. Do not drop inapplicable entries from those percentages and renormalize the resulting flat list.
weight_allocation.calibration_note: These weights are initial design values, not proportions prescribed by the Word standard, and have not yet been calibrated against the new 100-case set.

applicability.amendment_rule: G3-G5 activate together when the candidate actually amends the claims and are scored using the Word levels. If the synchronized zero-score rule applies, all three remain active with score 0. Otherwise, when no amendment is made, all three are not_applicable.
applicability.argument_rule: Determine applicability of each G6 criterion from the complete OA, the actual points of dispute, the jurisdiction, and the necessary reasoning steps. A single inventive-step objection may require several subcriteria. A missing candidate response does not make an existing issue not applicable.
applicability.not_applicable: Use status=not_applicable and score=null only when a conditional criterion does not apply; provide the reason and references to source materials. Only not_applicable releases allocated weight.

amendment_zero_rule.trigger: The Judge determines that the claims should be amended, but the candidate OAR has not chosen an amendment strategy.
amendment_zero_rule.evidence_requirement: Each of G3-G5 must cite the case basis showing why amendment is needed and evidence that the candidate did not choose that strategy. A difference between pre_claim and post_claim alone is insufficient to infer that amendment is required.
amendment_zero_rule.defect_description_requirement: Each criterion's defect description must identify its current metric ID and explain that the zero score is required by this synchronized rule.
amendment_zero_rule.scope: Do not mark these three criteria not_applicable or redistribute the amendment budget. G2, G6, and all other scoring rules continue to apply as specified.

result_contract.scored: A score of 0, 0.5, or 1 and verifiable evidence references are required.
result_contract.unscored: not_applicable, not_evaluable, and failed require score=null. Conditional not_applicable results require a reason and source references.
result_contract.failure_handling: not_evaluable and failed retain their allocated shares and block the final score. Do not redistribute their shares to scored criteria or remove an inventive-step type because one subcriterion cannot be evaluated.
result_contract.consistency_checks: Validate required criteria, consistent applicability of G3-G5, compliance with the synchronized zero-score rule, and evidence fields. Programmatic checks do not replace semantic review.

audit_fields.common_group_allocation: Group budgets, active criteria, and argument.types with issue-type budgets and subcriteria.
audit_fields.common_allocated_weights: Allocated weights including shares reserved for not_evaluable or failed criteria.
audit_fields.common_effective_weights: Weights actually contributing to the score; not_applicable, not_evaluable, and failed have effective weight 0. Failed or unevaluable applicable criteria still block a final total.

scoring_policy.duplicate_defect_rule: Assign each minimal defect to one primary criterion rather than penalizing it repeatedly across criteria. The explicitly required synchronized G3-G5 zero scores are a policy exception; each must identify the current criterion and the reason for the rule-based zero score.

levels.0.5: Correctly assesses the main technical solution, the grounds for objection, and the points open to argument, but has localized misunderstandings of noncritical facts, feature relationships, or document content; these do not change the main direction of the response and can be corrected locally.
levels.0: Misunderstands the technical solution of the application, feature relationships, or the Office Action; makes errors such as confusing the original claims, the current claims, and the proposed amended claims.

**<u>Art. 123(2), 76(1) EPC</u>**

Dependent **claim 2** does not fulfill the requirements of Article 76(1) EPC since the parent application does not disclose a **"U-shaped connector"**, in a <u>generalized way</u>, between the **"gas stop valve (5)"** and the **"gas filter (6)"**. In his letter of 26 April 2021, the applicant states that a U-shaped connector is disclosed in Fig. 4, where it is shown as connecting elements with reference numerals 5 and 6. However, Fig. 4 shows a detailed embodiment disclosing a realization of a complete part of the outdoor unit with various mutual connections between individual elements which cannot be structurally and functionally separated from the inverted **"U-shaped"** connection between the **"gas stop valve (5)"** and the **"gas filter (6)"**. The amendment therefore represents an inadmissible intermediate generalization (Guidelines H-V 3.2.1). It is therefore proposed to delete present dependent **claim 2**.

**<u>Art. 54 and 56 EPC</u>**

The subject-matter of independent **claim 1** is not new (Article 54 EPC) in view of the disclosure of document **D1**. The arguments put forward by the applicant in his letter dated 26 April 2021 do not allay these objections.

With respect to the arguments presented by the applicant in his letter, his attention is drawn to the fact that, under Article 84 EPC, the features of the claims are to be given the broadest meaning given to them by the person skilled in the art. If a feature is to have a more particular meaning based on the description, amendment of the claims is to be carried out (Guidelines F-IV 4.2). In its broadest possibility of interpretation, the person skilled in the art will understand based on his general technical knowledge that a **"flow path that extends in a horizontal direction"** also corresponds to a horizontal direction of a flow path which only forms a sub-part of a larger, overall vertical flow-path. With respect to **D1**, this is the case in view of the horizontal flow across filter element 74c, see Figure 5(B).

Summarizing, therefore, the subject-matter of present independent **claim 1** is not new (Article 54 EPC) in view of the disclosure of document D1. Document D1 (see Figures 1, 3, 5) shows an outdoor unit (*D1: 1a*) suitable for use as part of a heat pump, the outdoor unit comprising: a package that defines a chamber (*D1: engine room 102 and heat exchange chamber 101*); a liquid stop valve (*D1: stop valve 73*) disposed in the chamber; and a liquid filter (*D1: filter 74*) disposed in the chamber, the liquid filter (*D1: filter 74*) being connected to the liquid stop valve (*D1: stop valve 73*) and configured to be connected, via a liquid pipe (*D1: 48*), to an indoor unit (*D1: 1b*) of the heat pump, a compressor (*D1: 20*) disposed in the chamber (*D1: implicitly in the engine room 102, where it is connected to engine 2, also see paragraph [0011]*); a gas stop valve (*D1: valve 77, arranged upstream from the strainer 78 and upstream from the joint 47 between the outdoor unit 1a and the gas transfer line 49, see Figure 1*) disposed in the chamber (*D1: see Figure 3*); and a gas filter (*D1: 78*) disposed in the chamber (*D1: see Figure 3*), the gas filter (*D1: 78*) being connected to the gas stop valve (*D1: 77*) and configured to be connected, via a gas pipe (*D1: 49*), to the indoor unit (*D1: 1b*) of the heat pump; wherein the liquid stop valve (*D1: stop valve 73*) has a flow path that extends in an up-down direction (*D1: see Figure 3, flow path from inlet towards outlet arranged overall vertically*) and the liquid filter (*D1: filter 74*) has a flow path that extends in a horizontal direction (*D1: see Figure 5(B) where <u>the flow path inside the filter across filter element 74C is horizontal</u>*); a gas flow path (*D1: 30, 41, 45*) is further defined from the compressor (*D1: 20*) to the gas stop valve (*D1: 77*), and from the gas stop valve (*D1: 77*) to the gas filter (*D1: 78*), and the gas filter (*D1: 78*) to the indoor unit (*D1: 1b*)

**<u>In order to arrive at a subject-matter that may fulfill the requirements of the EPC with respect of novelty and inventive step (Articles 54 and 56 EPC) with respect to the closest prior art shown by document D1 and in further view of D2, it is proposed to</u>** include the subject-matter of dependent **claim 3** and the additional optional feature of "overlapping height range[s]" of paragraph [0012] of the **originally filed description** in the subject-matter of independent **claim 1**. These features would solve the problem of improved mountability and reduced space requirements and thereby fulfill the advantages addressed by the applicant in his letter of 26 April 2021.

Of course, the applicant may also amend the independent claim differently, as long as the resulting subject-matter represents an inventive contribution over the cited prior art and complies with the further requirements of the EPC. When amending the application, the applicant should ensure that the requirements of Article 123(2) EPC are fulfilled, particularly <u>avoiding inadmissible intermediate generalizations</u> (see the Guidelines H-V 3.2.1).

**<u>FURTHER COMMENTS</u>**

The subject-matter of dependent **claim 3** is also not new (Article 54 EPC) in view of document **D1** (see Figures 3, 5), which also shows an overall up-down, i.e. overall vertical, orientation of both filter and valve.

Notwithstanding its failure to comply with the requirements of Article 123(2) EPC, see above, the subject-matter of dependent **claim 2** is obvious (Article 56 EPC) in view of the closest prior art shown by document **D1**. The skilled person is aware of the possibility of connecting the gas stop valve and the gas filter to each other via a U-shaped connector from his **general technical knowledge** for compensating thermal expansion, and will apply this to the configuration of document **D1** without inventive skill if the circumstances make this desirable.

When submitting an amended set of claims, the applicant should take into account all of the objections raised above and further the following points:

1 The independent claims should be **brought into two-part form** as required by Rule 43(1) EPC.
